docs.title: 13.1. Installation of Node.js
docs.text:
[Node.js] is downloaded to nodejs.org: select version LTS (long-term support), 20 or higher. The [Windows] installer also installs [npm]. Verify the installation in a console ([PowerShell] or command prompt):

node --version
npm --version

The examples do not require installing the [nest] tool globally: it is included as a dependency in the [exemples] folder and the case study, and can be accessed via [npx nest].

docs.title: 13.2. Installing Visual Studio Code
docs.text: [Visual Studio Code] is downloaded from code.visualstudio.com. It includes [TypeScript] without an extension. For views, the Handlebars extension (syntax highlighting for [.hbs] files) is useful. Open the [exemples] folder (File menu / Open Folder); the built-in terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal) allows you to run the [npm] and [npx] commands without leaving the editor.

docs.title: 13.3. Installing MySQL with Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] (laragon.org) installs a [MySQL] server (or [MariaDB]) ready for use, along with the [HeidiSQL] administration tool. After installation:

  • the "Start All" button launches the [MySQL] server on port 3306;
  • the user [root] has no password: these are the default values from Example 28;
  • the "Database" button opens [HeidiSQL], where the File / Run File SQL runs the scripts [dbpersonnes.sql] (Example 28) and [dbrdvmedecins2.sql] (case study).

In [Linux] or [macOS], install [MySQL] or [MariaDB] using the system’s package manager, and then run the scripts using the command-line client [mysql].

docs.title: 13.4. Installing curl
docs.text: [curl] is included with [Windows] 10 and 11, [macOS], and most [Linux] distributions. On [PowerShell], you must type [curl.exe], not [curl]: In older versions of [PowerShell], [curl] is an alias for another command ([Invoke-WebRequest]), which has different options.

docs.title: 8. Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
Two distinct questions arise for each request:

  • Who is the user? This is authentication: the user has identified themselves with a username and password, and every subsequent request must prove that it comes from them;
  • Do they have permission to access this page? This is authorization: in the case study, only a user with the role ADMIN manages doctors and clients.

Since the server is stateless (Chapter 6), proof of identity must be included with every request. A token JWT ([JSON Web Token]) is used: after login, the server generates a token containing the user’s identity and signs it with a secret key. The token is stored in a cookie; the browser sends it back with every request; the server verifies the signature. The user can read their token but cannot modify it: any modification invalidates the signature.

[NestJS] relies on two libraries for this: [passport] (and its strategy [passport-jwt]), which verifies tokens, and [@nestjs/jwt], which generates them.

The file [src/auth/constantes.ts]:

// the name of the cookie that carries the token
export const COOKIE_JWT = 'jeton';
// the secret key that signs the tokens (in production: an environment variable)
export const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET ?? 'secret-de-developpement';
// token lifetime, in seconds
export const JWT_DUREE = 3600;

Line 4: the key that signs the tokens. Anyone who knows this key can generate valid tokens: in production, it comes from an environment variable, never from the source code.

The file [src/auth/utilisateurs.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import * as bcrypt from 'bcryptjs';

export interface Utilisateur {
  id: number;
  login: string;
  nom: string;
  role: 'ADMIN' | 'USER';
  motDePasseHache: string; // JAMAIS the password itself
}

// users, in memory (the next chapter will store them in the database).
// Each user’s password is their login; only its bcrypt hash is stored
@Injectable()
export class UtilisateursService {
  private readonly utilisateurs: Utilisateur[] = [
    { id: 1, login: 'admin', nom: 'Administrateur', role: 'ADMIN', motDePasseHache: bcrypt.hashSync('admin', 10) },
    { id: 2, login: 'marie', nom: 'Marie Pélissier', role: 'USER', motDePasseHache: bcrypt.hashSync('marie', 10) },
  ];

  parLogin(login: string): Utilisateur | undefined {
    return this.utilisateurs.find((u) => u.login === login);
  }
}
  • Line 9: We never store a password; we only store its hash—a fingerprint calculated by a one-way function. We can verify that a password matches a fingerprint, but we cannot recover the password from the fingerprint;
  • Lines 16–19: [bcrypt.hashSync(motDePasse, 10)] calculates the hash using the [bcrypt] algorithm. The number 10 represents the “cost”: bcrypt is intentionally slow (2¹⁰ iterations) to discourage anyone from trying millions of passwords. Two hashes of the same password are different (a random “salt” is added): [bcrypt.compare] is responsible for verifying them.

The file [src/auth/auth.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtService } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import * as bcrypt from 'bcryptjs';
import { Utilisateur, UtilisateursService } from './utilisateurs.service';

// what the token contains: enough information to identify the user without querying the database
export interface ContenuJeton {
  sub: number; // "subject": the user’s identifier (convention: JWT)
  login: string;
  nom: string;
  role: string;
}

@Injectable()
export class AuthService {
  constructor(
    private readonly utilisateurs: UtilisateursService,
    private readonly jwt: JwtService,
  ) {}

   // the user if the username/password pair is correct; null otherwise
  async verifier(login: string, motDePasse: string): Promise<Utilisateur | null> {
    const u = this.utilisateurs.parLogin(login);
     // bcrypt.compare hashes the entered password and compares the hashes
    return u && (await bcrypt.compare(motDePasse, u.motDePasseHache)) ? u : null;
  }

   // a token SIGNÉ: the browser can read it, but not modify it
  creerJeton(u: Utilisateur): string {
    const contenu: ContenuJeton = { sub: u.id, login: u.login, nom: u.nom, role: u.role };
    return this.jwt.sign(contenu);
  }
}
  • lines 7–12: the token’s content. [sub] ([subject]) is the conventional name for the user ID. We include whatever the pages need (name, role) so we don’t have to query the database with every request;
  • lines 22–26: verification of the username and password;
  • lines 29–32: [JwtService.sign] generates the signed token. [JwtService] is configured (key, lifetime) in the application module.

The [src/auth/jwt.strategy.ts] file:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { Request } from 'express';
import { ExtractJwt, Strategy } from 'passport-jwt';
import { ContenuJeton } from './auth.service';
import { COOKIE_JWT, JWT_SECRET } from './constantes';

// the logged-in user, as seen by the controllers (req.user)
export interface UtilisateurConnecte {
  id: number;
  login: string;
  nom: string;
  role: string;
}

// Passport’s “jwt” strategy: where to find the token, how to verify it
@Injectable()
export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'jwt') {
  constructor() {
    super({
       // The token is read from the cookie (not from the Authorization header)
      jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromExtractors([(req: Request) => req?.cookies?.[COOKIE_JWT] ?? null]),
      ignoreExpiration: false, // An expired token is rejected
      secretOrKey: JWT_SECRET, // To verify the signature
    });
  }

   // called if the token is valid; what it returns becomes req.user
  validate(contenu: ContenuJeton): UtilisateurConnecte {
    return { id: contenu.sub, login: contenu.login, nom: contenu.nom, role: contenu.role };
  }
}
  • line 18: a [Passport] policy, named [jwt], describes how to authenticate a request;
  • line 22: where to find the token: in the cookie. (A [JavaScript] client would instead send it in the [Authorization: Bearer ...] header; see [ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken()]);
  • lines 23–24: an expired or incorrectly signed token is rejected;
  • lines 29–31: called when the token is valid. The result is [req.user]: the logged-in user, with access to actions.

The file [src/auth/jwt-auth.guard.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthGuard } from '@nestjs/passport';

// the guard that enforces the 'jwt' policy: no valid token -> 401
@Injectable()
export class JwtAuthGuard extends AuthGuard('jwt') {}

[AuthGuard('jwt')] creates a guard that executes the [jwt] policy. Without a valid token, it raises a [UnauthorizedException] (401).

The file [src/auth/auth.controller.ts]:

import { Body, Controller, Get, Post, Render, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';
import { COOKIE_JWT, JWT_DUREE } from './constantes';

@Controller()
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private readonly auth: AuthService) {}

  @Get('login')
  @Render('login')
  formulaire(): object {
    return {};
  }

  @Post('login')
  async connecter(@Body() corps: { login?: string; motDePasse?: string }, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    const utilisateur = await this.auth.verifier(corps.login ?? '', corps.motDePasse ?? '');
    if (!utilisateur) {
       // intentionally vague message: it does not specify which of the two is incorrect
      res.render('login', { login: corps.login, erreur: 'Login ou mot de passe incorrect.' });
      return;
    }
     // the token is stored in a cookie httpOnly: the JavaScript from the page
     // cannot read it; the browser sends it back with every request
    res.cookie(COOKIE_JWT, this.auth.creerJeton(utilisateur), {
      httpOnly: true,
      sameSite: 'lax',
      maxAge: JWT_DUREE * 1000,
    });
    res.redirect('/profil');
  }

   // logout MODIFIE status: it is a POST, not a link
  @Post('logout')
  deconnecter(@Res() res: Response): void {
    res.clearCookie(COOKIE_JWT);
    res.redirect('/login');
  }
}
  • lines 17–32: the login. If the login fails, the form is redisplayed with a deliberately vague message: stating “this login does not exist” would help an attacker find valid logins;
  • lines 26–30: if successful, the token is stored in a cookie named [httpOnly]; the page’s [JavaScript] cannot read it, which protects the token if a malicious script were to execute on the page. [sameSite: 'lax']: The cookie is not included in POST requests sent from another site, which protects against request forgery ([CSRF]);
  • Lines 35–39: Logging out deletes the cookie. This is a POST: it changes the user’s status (see Example 21).

The [src/profil.controller.ts] file:

import { Controller, Get, Render, Req, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request } from 'express';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from './auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { UtilisateurConnecte } from './auth/jwt.strategy';

@Controller()
export class ProfilController {
   // public page
  @Get()
  @Render('accueil')
  accueil(): object {
    return {};
  }

   // protected page: the guard requires a valid token
  @Get('profil')
  @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
  @Render('profil')
  profil(@Req() req: Request): object {
    return { utilisateur: req.user as UtilisateurConnecte };
  }
}

Line 17: The page [/profil] is protected by the guard. The action reads the user from [req.user].

The file [src/erreurs.filter.ts]:

import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpException, HttpStatus } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';

@Catch(HttpException)
export class ErreursFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  catch(exception: HttpException, host: ArgumentsHost): void {
    const res = host.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const status = exception.getStatus();
     // 401 (no token, or invalid token): redirect to the login page
    if (status === HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED) {
      res.redirect('/login');
      return;
    }
    res.status(status).render('erreur', { status, message: exception.message });
  }
}

Lines 10–13: A 401 error does not display an error page; the user is redirected to the login page.

The file [src/app.module.ts]:

import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtModule } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { PassportModule } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { AuthController } from './auth/auth.controller';
import { AuthService } from './auth/auth.service';
import { JWT_DUREE, JWT_SECRET } from './auth/constantes';
import { JwtStrategy } from './auth/jwt.strategy';
import { UtilisateursService } from './auth/utilisateurs.service';
import { ProfilController } from './profil.controller';

@Module({
  imports: [
    PassportModule,
     // JwtService, configured once and for all: key and lifetime
    JwtModule.register({ secret: JWT_SECRET, signOptions: { expiresIn: JWT_DUREE } }),
  ],
  controllers: [AuthController, ProfilController],
  providers: [UtilisateursService, AuthService, JwtStrategy],
})
export class AppModule {}

Line 15: the configuration of [JwtService]: token key and lifetime (one hour).

The file [views/login.hbs]:

docs.title: 8.1.1. Execution
docs.text:
Without a cookie, the protected page redirects to the login page:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /login
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

Found. Redirecting to /login

An incorrect password:

Successful login, as seen by [curl]:

curl -i -c cookies.txt -d "login=marie&motDePasse=marie" http://localhost:3000/login

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Set-Cookie: jeton=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOjIsImxvZ2luIjoibWFyaWUiLCJub20iOiJNYXJpZSBQw6lsaXNzaWVyIiwicm9sZSI6IlVTRVIiLCJpYXQiOjE3OTAxNzMwODcsImV4cCI6MTc5MDE3NjY4N30.ThiPopT9JH3D3CwHTSn3w5Z3CrJP9PYNvLl6gYH4DCI; Max-Age=3600; Path=/; Expires=Wed, 23 Sep 2026 15:18:07 GMT; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Location: /profil
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 29

Found. Redirecting to /profil

The token consists of three parts separated by periods: a header, the content, and the signature. The first two are simply encoded as [base64url]; let’s decode the content:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOjIsImxvZ2luIjoibWFyaWUiLCJub20iOiJNYXJpZSBQw6lsaXNzaWVyIiwicm9sZSI6IlVTRVIiLCJpYXQiOjE3OTAxNzMwODcsImV4cCI6MTc5MDE3NjY4N30.ThiPopT9JH3D3CwHTSn3w5Z3CrJP9PYNvLl6gYH4DCI

{"sub": 2, "login": "marie", "nom": "Marie Pélissier", "role": "USER", "iat": 1790173087, "exp": 1790176687}

The content generated by [creerJeton] is included, along with two fields added by [JwtService]: [iat] ([issued at], the creation date) and [exp] (the expiration date), in seconds since January 1, 1970. The token is not encrypted: it does not contain any confidential information. In the browser:

Now let’s try to modify the token to assign ourselves the role ADMIN: we decode the content, replace [USER] with [ADMIN], and re-encode it… but we can’t recalculate the signature without the secret key:

curl -i -b "jeton=eyJhbGciOi...(contenu modifié)...ThiPopT9..." http://localhost:3000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /login
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

Found. Redirecting to /login

The signature no longer matches the content: the token is rejected (error 401), and the exception handler redirects to the login page. Logging out:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -X POST http://localhost:3000/logout

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Set-Cookie: jeton=; Path=/; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT
Location: /login
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

Found. Redirecting to /login

docs.title: 8.2. Example 26: Roles
docs.text:
Example 26 builds on Example 25 and adds a page reserved for the role ADMIN. Three new files have been added.

The file [src/auth/roles.decorator.ts]:

import { SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';

export const CLE_ROLES = 'roles';

// @Roles('ADMIN'): applies a MÉTADONNÉE to the action (or controller);
// the decorator does not check anything itself; RolesGuard will read it
export const Roles = (...roles: string[]) => SetMetadata(CLE_ROLES, roles);

Line 7: [SetMetadata] attaches metadata (any information) to the decorated class or method. [@Roles('ADMIN')] does not check anything: it declares the required role.

The file [src/auth/roles.guard.ts]:

import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Request } from 'express';
import { UtilisateurConnecte } from './jwt.strategy';
import { CLE_ROLES } from './roles.decorator';

@Injectable()
export class RolesGuard implements CanActivate {
   // Reflector: the tool used by NestJS to re-read the metadata
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(contexte: ExecutionContext): boolean {
     // @Roles of the action; otherwise, those of the controller
    const requis = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>(CLE_ROLES, [contexte.getHandler(), contexte.getClass()]);
    if (!requis || requis.length === 0) {
      return true; // No @Roles: no role restrictions
    }
     // req.user was submitted by JwtAuthGuard, which executes AVANT this guard
    const utilisateur = contexte.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>().user as UtilisateurConnecte;
    if (!requis.includes(utilisateur.role)) {
      throw new ForbiddenException(`le rôle ${utilisateur.role} ne donne pas accès à cette page`);
    }
    return true;
  }
}
  • line 10: [Reflector] is the service for [NestJS] that reads the metadata;
  • line 14: the roles required by the action, or failing that, by its controller. This is where the guard’s execution context comes into play (see Chapter 7);
  • lines 15–17: without [@Roles], there are no restrictions;
  • line 19: [req.user] was registered by the guard [JwtAuthGuard], which executes before it;
  • lines 20–22: an insufficient role causes a 403 (Forbidden) error.

The file [src/admin.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get, Render, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from './auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { Roles } from './auth/roles.decorator';
import { RolesGuard } from './auth/roles.guard';

// The order is as follows: first, QUI (JwtAuthGuard), then A-T-IL LE DROIT (RolesGuard)
@Controller('admin')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, RolesGuard)
@Roles('ADMIN')
export class AdminController {
  @Get()
  @Render('admin')
  admin(): object {
    return {};
  }
}

lines 8–9: guards are executed in the order in which they are listed: first the identification, then the role check. The entire controller is reserved for the role ADMIN. The user [marie] (role USER) attempts to open the administration page:

Same attempt by [admin]:

The case study has three roles (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER) and uses exactly these two guards. The exception filter converts the 403 into a translated error page.

docs.title: 8.3. Example 27: CAPTCHA and attempt limits
docs.text:
A login page attracts bots: programs that try thousands of login/password combinations. Two complementary safeguards:

  • a CAPTCHA: an image of distorted characters that a human can read easily but that a simple bot cannot decipher;
  • an attempt limit: after a few failed attempts, the address IP is blocked for a while.

Example 27 adds these two safeguards to Example 25.

The file [src/auth/captcha.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { randomUUID } from 'crypto';
import * as svgCaptcha from 'svg-captcha';

export interface Captcha {
  id: string; // placed in a hidden field of the form
  svg: string; // the image, inserted as-is into the page
}

@Injectable()
export class CaptchaService {
   // id -> expected response. The response does not leave the server (JAMAIS)
  private readonly reponses = new Map<string, string>();

  generer(): Captcha {
     // svg-captcha: random text rendered in distorted characters
    const { text, data } = svgCaptcha.create({ size: 5, noise: 3, color: true, ignoreChars: '0oO1iIlL' });
    const id = randomUUID();
    this.reponses.set(id, text.toLowerCase());
    return { id, svg: data };
  }

   // Is the answer correct? In any case, the CAPTCHA is
   // used up: an image can only be used once
  verifier(id: unknown, saisie: unknown): boolean {
    if (typeof id !== 'string' || typeof saisie !== 'string') {
      return false;
    }
    const attendue = this.reponses.get(id);
    this.reponses.delete(id);
    return attendue !== undefined && attendue === saisie.trim().toLowerCase();
  }
}
  • Line 13: The expected responses are stored by the server under a random identifier. The page contains only the image and the identifier: the response never leaves the server;
  • lines 15–21: The [svg-captcha] library generates a random text string and renders it as an image (SVG), obscured by lines. Characters that are easily confused (0 and O, 1 and l, etc.) are excluded;
  • lines 25–32: The verification process consumes the CAPTCHA: an image is used only once; a bot cannot reuse a response it has already found.

The file [src/auth/limiteur.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

const MAX_ECHECS = 3; // Failures are allowed...
const BLOCAGE_MS = 60 * 1000; // ... before a one-minute lockout

// limits the number of login attempts per address IP
@Injectable()
export class LimiteurService {
  private readonly compteurs = new Map<string, { echecs: number; bloqueJusqua: number }>();

   // 0 if the IP can try again; otherwise, the number of seconds to wait
  secondesDeBlocage(ip: string): number {
    const c = this.compteurs.get(ip);
    const reste = c ? c.bloqueJusqua - Date.now() : 0;
    return reste > 0 ? Math.ceil(reste / 1000) : 0;
  }

  echec(ip: string): void {
    const c = this.compteurs.get(ip) ?? { echecs: 0, bloqueJusqua: 0 };
    c.echecs++;
    if (c.echecs >= MAX_ECHECS) {
      c.bloqueJusqua = Date.now() + BLOCAGE_MS;
      c.echecs = 0;
    }
    this.compteurs.set(ip, c);
  }

  reussite(ip: string): void {
    this.compteurs.delete(ip);
  }
}
  • lines 3–4: Three failures block the address IP for one minute;
  • lines 12–16: the remaining block time;
  • lines 18–26 and 28–30: a failure is counted; a success resets the counter to zero.

The file [src/auth/auth.controller.ts]:

import { Body, Controller, Get, Ip, Post, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';
import { CaptchaService } from './captcha.service';
import { COOKIE_JWT, JWT_DUREE } from './constantes';
import { LimiteurService } from './limiteur.service';

interface CorpsLogin {
  login?: string;
  motDePasse?: string;
  captchaId?: string;
  captcha?: string;
}

@Controller()
export class AuthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly auth: AuthService,
    private readonly captchas: CaptchaService,
    private readonly limiteur: LimiteurService,
  ) {}

  @Get('login')
  formulaire(@Res() res: Response): void {
    this.afficher(res, {});
  }

  @Post('login')
  async connecter(@Body() corps: CorpsLogin, @Ip() ip: string, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
     // 1. A blocked IP isn't even listened to
    const secondes = this.limiteur.secondesDeBlocage(ip);
    if (secondes > 0) {
      this.afficher(res, { login: corps.login, erreur: `Trop de tentatives : réessayez dans ${secondes} s.` });
      return;
    }
     // 2. the CAPTCHA, then 3. the username and password
    const captchaOk = this.captchas.verifier(corps.captchaId, corps.captcha);
    const utilisateur = captchaOk ? await this.auth.verifier(corps.login ?? '', corps.motDePasse ?? '') : null;
    if (!utilisateur) {
      this.limiteur.echec(ip);
      const erreur = captchaOk ? 'Login ou mot de passe incorrect.' : 'Les caractères recopiés sont incorrects.';
      this.afficher(res, { login: corps.login, erreur });
      return;
    }
    this.limiteur.reussite(ip);
    res.cookie(COOKIE_JWT, this.auth.creerJeton(utilisateur), {
      httpOnly: true,
      sameSite: 'lax',
      maxAge: JWT_DUREE * 1000,
    });
    res.redirect('/profil');
  }

  @Post('logout')
  deconnecter(@Res() res: Response): void {
    res.clearCookie(COOKIE_JWT);
    res.redirect('/login');
  }

   // Each time the form is displayed, it has a NOUVEAU CAPTCHA
  private afficher(res: Response, modele: object): void {
    res.render('login', { ...modele, captcha: this.captchas.generer() });
  }
}
  • line 29: [@Ip()] injects the client’s address IP;
  • lines 32–35: a blocked IP is not even processed;
  • lines 37–38: the CAPTCHA is verified first; the password (which requires a computationally expensive bcrypt calculation) is only checked if the CAPTCHA is correct;
  • lines 39–44: an incorrect CAPTCHA counts as a failure;
  • lines 61–63: each time the form is displayed, a new CAPTCHA is generated.

docs.title: 11.1. The Problem
docs.text:
The RdvMedecins application manages appointments for a medical practice. Each doctor has time slots (from 8:00 AM to 12:00 PM in 20-minute increments, for example); an appointment consists of a day, a time slot, and a client (a patient). It uses the database and business layers from the [NestJS] server in the courses “An Example of a Flutter Client/Server / NestJS” and “An Example of an Angular Client/Server / NestJS, and displays the same pages as the [Angular] client; but instead of serving JSON to a client [JavaScript] or [Flutter], it generates its own HTML pages.

Three user roles share the application:

RoleWhoWhat they can doADMINThe administrator ([admin])view schedules, make and cancel appointments for any patient; manage (list, add, edit, delete) doctors and clientsDOCTORDoctorsView schedules, book, and cancel appointments for any patientUSERclients (patients)view schedules without seeing other patients’ names; book an appointment for themselves; cancel their appointment; manage their account; create an account

Key management rules:

  • No appointments in the past;
  • a time slot can only be booked once per day;
  • a patient may have only one upcoming appointment at a time;
  • Two doctors (or two clients) cannot have the same first and last names, and a login belongs to only one account;
  • A doctor with appointments cannot be deleted; A client is deleted along with their appointments;
  • the login page is protected against bots (CAPTCHA, limited attempts), and creating a client account requires first solving the CAPTCHA on that page.

docs.title: 11.4. Application Architecture
docs.text:
• [src/main.ts] configures the application: view engine, static files, cookies, exception filter;
  • [src/auth]: authentication, tokens (JWT), roles, CAPTCHA, and attempt limits;
  • [src/web]: the web layer. Its controllers ([src/web/controllers]) all pass through a single service, [ApplicationModelService], which stores the lists of doctors and clients in memory and forwards other requests to the business layer;
  • [src/metier]: the business rules;
  • [src/repositories]: the DAO layer, one class per table;
  • [src/entities]: the entities [TypeORM]; [src/domain]: the calendar objects, calculated by the business layer;
  • [views]: the views [Handlebars]; [i18n]: the dictionaries; [public]: the style sheet and the page script.

The suite comments on all files, from the lower layers (database) to the upper layers (views).

docs.title: 11.5. The database
docs.text:
The file [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql]:

-- =========================================================================
-- [dbrdvmedecins2] Database - MySQL 8
--
-- Changes to [dbrdvmedecins]:
--    1. The tables [medecins] and [clients] are added with a column named [user],
--       foreign key to users(id): every doctor and every client is
--       now also a user capable of logging in;
--    2. A third role appears: DOCTOR (in addition to ADMIN and USER);
--    3. The script creates a row [users] for each doctor (role DOCTOR)
--       and for each client (role USER):
--         -        login = name in lowercase
--         - password = name in lowercase, hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds)
--         - displ ay name = first name + last name
--
--    4. uniqueness constraints, all NOMMÉES (the application NestJS recognizes
--       the name of the violated constraint in the error message MySQL):
--         - unq_users         _login : a login belongs to only one account;
--         - unq_medecins_pren om_nom : Two doctors cannot have the
--                                      same first and last names;
--         - unq_clients_pren  om_nom : the same applies to clients.
--       Note: the utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation compares without taking into account
--       capital letters or accents—"Hélène DUPONT" and "helene dupont"
--       are therefore considered identical.
--
-- The table [users] must now be created AVANT [medecins] and [clients]
-- (they reference it), and deleted APRÈS them.
-- =========================================================================

-- the database is reset to empty each time the script runs (useful during development)
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins2 CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins2;

-- deletion order: from “child” tables to “parent” tables
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rv;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS creneaux;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS medecins;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: users authorized to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- login ID
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- password HACHÉ (bcrypt) — never stored in plain text
  nom      VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- display name after login
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- 'ADMIN', 'DOCTOR', or 'USER'
   -- A login can belong to only one account
  CONSTRAINT unq_users_login UNIQUE (login)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [medecins]: the practice’s doctors
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE medecins (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,      -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,               -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,                 -- Ms., Mrs., Mr.
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`  INT NOT NULL,                         -- Foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_medecins_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
   -- one account per doctor, and one doctor per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_medecins_user UNIQUE (`user`),
   -- No two doctors can have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_medecins_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: doctors' patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`  INT NOT NULL,                         -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_clients_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
   -- One account per customer, and one customer per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_user UNIQUE (`user`),
   -- Two clients cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [creneaux]: each doctor’s appointment slots
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE creneaux (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  id_medecin INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  hdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start time of the time slot
  mdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start minute of the time slot
  hfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- slot end hour
  mfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- end minute of the time slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_creneaux_medecin FOREIGN KEY (id_medecin) REFERENCES medecins(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [rv]: appointments made by customers
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE rv (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  jour       DATE NOT NULL,                      -- appointment date
  id_creneau INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> time slots (id)
  id_client  INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> customers(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_creneau FOREIGN KEY (id_creneau) REFERENCES creneaux(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_client  FOREIGN KEY (id_client)  REFERENCES clients(id),
   -- The same time slot on the same day can only be booked once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE (jour, id_creneau)
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

-- Users: Passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds of salting)
--    admin/admin (ADMIN)
--    One account (DOCTOR) per doctor, one account (USER) per client
--    (the demo account user/user has been removed: a USER account is
--    now TOUJOURS, which belongs to a client who can make reservations and manage their account)
--    (username = password = name in lowercase)

Let’s comment on this script:

  • line 30: as in Example 28, the collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] ignores uppercase letters and accents in comparisons;
  • lines 34–38: tables are deleted from the “child” tables to the “parent” tables: a table referenced by a foreign key cannot be deleted before the tables that reference it;
  • lines 43–52: user accounts. [password] contains the bcrypt hash of the password (see Example 25). Line 51: a login is unique;
  • Lines 57–69: Doctors. Each has an account (column [user], foreign key to [users], line 64). The name [user] is a reserved word for [MySQL]: it is enclosed in backticks. Line 66: an account belongs to only one doctor; line 68: no two doctors can have the same first and last names;
  • lines 74–86: clients, following the same format;
  • lines 91–100: each doctor’s time slots (start and end times in hours and minutes);
  • lines 105–115: appointments: one day, one time slot, one client. Line 114: a time slot is reserved only once per day;
  • lines 127–137: demo accounts; each account’s password is its login;
  • lines 141–144: each doctor’s [user] column is retrieved via a subquery on the login, rather than assuming the generated credentials;
  • lines 167–168: a same-day appointment ([CURDATE()]), to immediately show a booked time slot.

The [src/config/database.config.ts] file:

// =========================================================================
// config/database.config.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Configuration of the database connection MySQL, used by
// TypeORM. This is equivalent to the [DomainAndPersitenceConfig] class from the
// original Spring project, which defined a [DataSource] (@Bean block).
//
// Here, there is no class: NestJS/TypeORM prefers a simple function that
// returns a configuration object, read from the environment variables
// (the .env file in the project root, automatically loaded by NestJS
// via the @nestjs/config module if it's installed—here we read it directly
// process.env to keep things simple and clear).
// =========================================================================

import { TypeOrmModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Medecin } from '../entities/medecin.entity';
import { Client } from '../entities/client.entity';
import { Creneau } from '../entities/creneau.entity';
import { Rv } from '../entities/rv.entity';
import { User } from '../entities/user.entity';

export function getDatabaseConfig(): TypeOrmModuleOptions {
  return {
     // 'mysql': we use the MySQL driver, just like the original project (MySQL5 -> MySQL8 here).
    type: 'mysql',
    host: process.env.DB_HOST ?? 'localhost',
    port: process.env.DB_PORT ? parseInt(process.env.DB_PORT, 10) : 3306,
    username: process.env.DB_USERNAME ?? 'root',
    password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD ?? '',
    database: process.env.DB_DATABASE ?? 'dbrdvmedecins2',

     // The list of entities (@Entity classes) that TypeORM must manage.
     // This is equivalent to the automatic “scan” of @Entity classes performed by Spring Boot.
    entities: [Medecin, Client, Creneau, Rv, User],

     // IMPORTANT: `synchronize=false` is set permanently in this course.
     // If `synchronize` were set to `true`, TypeORM would modify the database schema on its own
     // based on the entities: useful for a disposable prototype, but dangerous once you have
     // real data (risk of data loss). We prefer, as
     // a real team would, to maintain control over the schema via the script database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql.
    synchronize: false,

     // displays the SQL queries generated by TypeORM in the console: very useful for
     // understand what ORM is doing for you, just like the Hibernate logs
     // from the original Spring project.
    logging: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production',
  };
}

docs.title: 11.7. Starting the application
docs.text:
The file [src/main.ts]:

// =========================================================================
// main.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Application entry point. Compared to the server JSON, the
// startup also configures everything needed for FABRIQUER DES PAGES
// HTML on the server side:
//    - a view engine (Handlebars, views/*.hbs files);
//    - static files (Bootstrap, CSS, some JavaScript);
//    - reading cookies (JWT token, language, flash messages);
//    - a filter that converts errors into HTML pages.
// There is no longer a need to authorize CORS: pages and data now come
// from the MÊME server.
// =========================================================================

import 'dotenv/config'; // DOIT remains the very first import (see server JSON)
import 'reflect-metadata';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import * as cookieParser from 'cookie-parser';
import * as hbs from 'hbs';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { DOSSIER_BOOTSTRAP, DOSSIER_PARTIELS, DOSSIER_PUBLIC, DOSSIER_VUES } from './config/chemins';
import { enregistrerHelpers } from './web/vues/helpers-handlebars';
import { contexteVueMiddleware } from './web/contexte-vue';
import { HtmlExceptionFilter } from './web/html-exception.filter';
import { UtilisateurVueInterceptor } from './web/utilisateur-vue.interceptor';

async function bootstrap() {
   // NestExpressApplication: it is specified that the underlying platform is
   // Express, to access its specific methods (setViewEngine,
   // useStaticAssets...)—these do not exist for the Fastify platform.
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);

   // 1. static files: /css/..., /js/... (public/ folder) and
   /   / /bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css (directly from node_modules:
   /   / no need to copy Bootstrap into the project)
  app.useStaticAssets(DOSSIER_PUBLIC);
  app.useStaticAssets(DOSSIER_BOOTSTRAP, { prefix: '/bootstrap/' });

   // 2. The view engine. The file views/layout.hbs is used
   /   / AUTOMATIQUEMENT by hbs as a common template for all pages:
   /   / Each view is inserted at the {{{body}}} location in this template.
  app.setBaseViewsDir(DOSSIER_VUES);
  app.setViewEngine('hbs');
  enregistrerHelpers(hbs);
   // "partials" (views/partials/*.hbs): reusable page fragments,
   // inserted using {{> name}}. registerPartials reads the directory
   // asynchronously: we wait for it to finish before accepting requests.
  await new Promise<void>((fini) => hbs.registerPartials(DOSSIER_PARTIELS, () => fini()));

   // 3. cookie-parser populates req.cookies; then our middleware prepares the
   /   / language and flash message for each page (see web/contexte-vue.ts)
  app.use(cookieParser());
  app.use(contexteVueMiddleware);

   // 4. the logged-in user, visible on all views; and the errors
   /   / are converted into HTML pages (or redirected to /login)
  app.useGlobalInterceptors(new UtilisateurVueInterceptor());
  app.useGlobalFilters(new HtmlExceptionFilter());

  const port = process.env.PORT ? parseInt(process.env.PORT, 10) : 8081;
  await app.listen(port);
   // eslint-disable-next-line no-console
  console.log(`[RdvMedecins] application web démarrée sur http://localhost:${port}`);
}

bootstrap();

Let’s break down this code:

  • Line 15: [dotenv/config] reads the file [.env] and places its values into [process.env]. This import must be the first one: the other modules read [process.env] as soon as they are loaded ([JWT_SECRET], for example);
  • lines 37–38: static files (see Example 15);
  • lines 43–49: the view engine, helpers, and partial views (see Examples 15 and 16);
  • lines 53–54: reading cookies, followed by the middleware that prepares the language and flash message for each page (see [web/contexte-vue.ts]);
  • lines 58–59: a global interceptor exposes the logged-in user to the views, and a global filter converts exceptions into HTML pages (see Chapter 7);
  • line 61: the port, read from [.env] (8081 by default).

docs.title: 11.8. The entities
docs.text: The [TypeORM] entities map to the database tables and classes in [TypeScript] (see Example 28). Their comments often refer to the [Java] / [Spring] project, of which the application is a distant descendant, and to the “JSON server”: the [NestJS] server from the client/server courses, whose case study incorporates the DAO and business layers.

docs.title: 11.8.1. src/entities/abstract.entity.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/abstract.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent to the class [AbstractEntity] from the original Spring project,
// which was annotated with @MappedSuperclass. It combines the two fields
// common to all our persistent entities: the identifier [id] and the
// version number [version] used for managing concurrent access.
//
// In JPA, @MappedSuperclass indicates “this class is not a table,
// but its fields must be added to the tables of the child classes."
// TypeORM offers exactly the same mechanism: all that is required is for an
// (not annotated with @Entity) is inherited by a class that,
// in turn, carries the @Entity annotation. TypeORM then automatically adds
// the inherited columns to the child class’s table.
// =========================================================================

import { PrimaryGeneratedColumn, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

export abstract class AbstractEntity {
   // equivalent to:
   /  / @Id
   /  / @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.AUTO)
   /  / protected Long id;
  //
   // @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() declares an auto-incrementing primary key via SGBD,
   // exactly as GenerationType.AUTO did, delegating it to SGBD.
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn()
  id: number;

   // equivalent to:
   /  / @Version
   /  / protected Long version;
  //
   // @VersionColumn() is LE, the native mechanism of TypeORM for optimistic locking:
   // TypeORM automatically increments this column on every UPDATE, and raises an error
   // if you attempt to save an entity whose version no longer matches the one in
   // database (someone else has modified it in the meantime). This is a direct mapping to the
   // role of @Version in JPA/Hibernate.
  @VersionColumn()
  version: number;
}
  • line 19: an abstract class without a decorator [@Entity]: it does not correspond to any table, but its columns are added to those of the child classes;
  • lines 27–28: the primary key, generated by the database;
  • lines 39–40: the row version, incremented by [TypeORM] with each modification (optimistic lock; see Example 28).

docs.title: 11.8.2. src/entities/personne.entity.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/personne.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Parent class (not itself persistent) of the entities [Medecin] and
// [Client]: a title, a last name, a first name—and, new to the database
// [dbrdvmedecins2], the associated user account (column [user]).
//
// A relationship declared in an abstract class is inherited by the
// child classes in exactly the same way as columns: TypeORM therefore adds the
// relation [user] to the table [medecins] and ET to the table [clients].
// =========================================================================

import { Column, JoinColumn, OneToOne, RelationId } from 'typeorm';
import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';
import { User } from './user.entity';

export abstract class Personne extends AbstractEntity {
  @Column({ length: 5 })
  titre: string; // Miss, Mrs., Mr.

  @Column({ length: 20 })
  nom: string;

  @Column({ length: 20 })
  prenom: string;

   // @OneToOne: a doctor (or a client) has a UN user account, and a
   // user account belongs to at most UNE person (the [user] column
   // is set to UNIQUE in the script SQL).
   // @JoinColumn({ name: 'user' }): this is the CETTE table (doctors / clients)
   //, which contains the foreign key in the column named [user].
   // As with the other relationships, [user] is loaded only on demand
   // (`relations` option) — see medecin.repository.ts.
  @OneToOne(() => User)
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'user' })
  user: User;

   // the raw value of the foreign key, without loading the entire User
   // (same technique as Creneau.idMedecin; see creneau.entity.ts)
  @RelationId((personne: Personne) => personne.user)
  idUser: number;
}
  • line 17: the parent class of [Medecin] and [Client], itself a child of [AbstractEntity];
  • Lines 18–25: title, last name, first name;

// =========================================================================
// entities/medecin.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent of the entity JPA [Medecin]:
//
//    @Entity
//    @Table(name = "doctors")
//    public class Doctor extends Person { ... }
// =========================================================================

import { Entity, OneToMany, Unique } from 'typeorm';
import { Personne } from './personne.entity';
import { Creneau } from './creneau.entity';

// @Entity({ name: 'doctors' }): declares the class as an entity TypeORM,
// persisted in the table [medecins]. This is the exact equivalent of
// @Entity + @Table(name = "doctors") in JPA.
@Entity({ name: 'medecins' })
// reminder of the constraint SQL from the script database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql: two
// Doctors cannot have the same first and last names. As with unq1_rv
// (see rv.entity.ts), this is documentation: `synchronize=false` refers to the
// script SQL that actually creates the constraint—with the name CE, which the
// business layer recognizes in the MySQL error messages (see metier.service.ts).
@Unique('unq_medecins_prenom_nom', ['prenom', 'nom'])
export class Medecin extends Personne {
   // Reverse relationship (optional; useful for navigating from a doctor to their available time slots).
   // The original project did not define it on the [Medecin] side (only on the [Creneau] side),
   // but TypeORM makes it virtually effortless to add, and it is educationally useful:
   // it illustrates the "1 doctor -> multiple time slots" relationship in both directions.
  @OneToMany(() => Creneau, (creneau) => creneau.medecin)
  creneaux: Creneau[];
}
  • line 18: the class corresponds to the table [medecins];
  • line 24: the uniqueness constraint, included here for documentation purposes; it is actually created by the script SQL ([synchronize: false]);
  • Lines 30–31: the one-to-many relationship to the doctor’s time slots, the inverse of the relationship [@ManyToOne] from [Creneau].

docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/creneau.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent of the entity JPA [Creneau]:
//
//    @Entity
//    @Table(name = "slots")
//    public class Creneau extends AbstractEntity {
//        private int startHour, startMinute, endHour, endMinute;
//        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
//        @JoinColumn(name = "id_medecin")
//        private Doctor doctor;
//        @Column(name = "id_medecin", insertable = false, updatable = false)
//        private long idMedecin;
//   }
// =========================================================================

import { Column, Entity, JoinColumn, ManyToOne, RelationId } from 'typeorm';
import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';
import { Medecin } from './medecin.entity';

@Entity({ name: 'creneaux' })
export class Creneau extends AbstractEntity {
  @Column() hdebut: number; // slot start time
  @Column() mdebut: number; // slot start minute
  @Column() hfin: number; // slot end hour
  @Column() mfin: number; // slot end minute

   // equivalent to:
   /  / @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
   /  / @JoinColumn(name = "id_medecin")
   /  / private Doctor doctor;
  //
   // @ManyToOne: multiple time slots for the same doctor.
   // By default, TypeORM does not load the relationship [medecin] when reading a time slot
   // (default “lazy” behavior): you must explicitly request it using the option
   // `relations: ['medecin']` in a query—exactly as FetchType.LAZY required
   // to convert JPA to an explicit `left join fetch` in the query JPQL to retrieve the doctor.
  @ManyToOne(() => Medecin, (medecin) => medecin.creneaux)
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'id_medecin' })
  medecin: Medecin;

   // equivalent to:
   /  / @Column(name = "id_medecin", insertable = false, updatable = false)
   /  / private long idMedecin;
  //
   // @RelationId: this is the equivalent of EXACT and, in terms of TypeORM, the
   // "idMedecin" read-only field from the original project. It directly exposes the value
   // of the foreign key, SANS without needing to load the entire entity [Medecin].
   // Very useful for comparing identifiers without loading the related entities.
  @RelationId((creneau: Creneau) => creneau.medecin)
  idMedecin: number;
}
  • lines 24–27: the start and end hours and minutes;
  • lines 39–41: the many-to-one relationship to the doctor: multiple time slots for one doctor. The foreign key is the [id_medecin] column;
  • lines 51–52: the doctor’s ID, without loading the doctor.

docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/rv.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent to the entity JPA [Rv] (an appointment):
//
//    @Entity
//    @Table(name = "rv")
//    public class Rv extends AbstractEntity {
//        @Temporal(TemporalType.DATE) private Date day;
//        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @JoinColumn(name = "id_client") private Client client;
//        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @JoinColumn(name = "id_creneau") private Slot slot;
//        @Column(name = "id_client", insertable = false, updatable = false) private long idClient;
//        @Column(name = "id_creneau", insertable = false, updatable = false) private long idCreneau;
//   }
//
// The uniqueness constraint SQL on (day, id_creneau)—which prevents two
// appointments in the same time slot on the same day—is defined directly
// in the script database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql (CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE).
// =========================================================================

import { Column, Entity, JoinColumn, ManyToOne, RelationId, Unique } from 'typeorm';
import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';
import { Client } from './client.entity';
import { Creneau } from './creneau.entity';

@Entity({ name: 'rv' })
// refers, on the TypeORM side, to the SQL constraint in the BDD script. Note: here we are referring to
// the name of the RELATION ("slot"), not the field @RelationId ('idCreneau')—the latter is
// a “virtual” (calculated) column, which TypeORM does not accept in an @Unique constraint.
// TypeORM itself maps 'slot' to its actual foreign key column (id_creneau).
@Unique('unq1_rv', ['jour', 'creneau'])
export class Rv extends AbstractEntity {
   // equivalent to: @Temporal(TemporalType.DATE) private Date day;
   // 'date' type (not 'datetime'): only the day is retained, not the time,
   // exactly as specified by TemporalType.DATE on the JPA side.
  @Column({ type: 'date' })
  jour: string; // "yyyy-MM-dd" format, e.g., "2026-09-13"

  @ManyToOne(() => Client)
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'id_client' })
  client: Client;

  @ManyToOne(() => Creneau)
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'id_creneau' })
  creneau: Creneau;

   // read-only equivalents of the idClient / idCreneau fields from the original project
   // (see detailed explanation in creneau.entity.ts regarding @RelationId)
  @RelationId((rv: Rv) => rv.client)
  idClient: number;

  @RelationId((rv: Rv) => rv.creneau)
  idCreneau: number;
}
  • line 31: an appointment slot is reserved only once per day;
  • lines 36–37: a column of type [DATE], treated as a string [aaaa-mm-jj]: no time zone issues, and two dates are compared as strings;
  • lines 39–45: the client and the appointment time slot;
  • lines 49–53: their IDs.

// =========================================================================
// entities/user.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A user authorized to log in to the application (table [users]).
//
// New feature in the [dbrdvmedecins2] database: every doctor and every client
// now has a user account (column [user] in tables
// [medecins] and [clients]; see personne.entity.ts). Hence a third role:
//    - ADMI N: the administrator—schedules appointments and manages doctors and clients;
//    - DOCTOR: a doctor—schedules and cancels appointments;
//    - USE  R : a client (patient)—books appointments for themselves, manages their account.
//
// The roles remain mutually exclusive: a single column [role]
// is always sufficient (no [roles] / [users_roles] tables as in the
// original Spring project).
// =========================================================================

import { Column, Entity, Unique } from 'typeorm';
import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';

export type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'DOCTOR' | 'USER';

@Entity({ name: 'users' })
// a login belongs to only one account (constraint SQL unq_users_login)
@Unique('unq_users_login', ['login'])
export class User extends AbstractEntity {
  @Column({ length: 30 })
  login: string;

   // the password HACHÉ (bcrypt) — never stored in plain text
  @Column({ length: 100 })
  password: string;

   // the display name after logging in—for a doctor or a client:
   // "first name NOM" (e.g., "Marie PELISSIER")
  @Column({ length: 40 })
  nom: string;

  @Column({ type: 'varchar', length: 10 })
  role: Role;
}
  • line 21: a union type of strings: a variable of type [Role] can only be one of these three strings;
  • lines 31–32: the password hash;
  • lines 36–37: the name displayed in the navigation bar (“Marie PELISSIER”);
  • lines 39–40: the role. The column type is specified: [TypeORM] cannot infer a type SQL from a union type.

docs.title: 11.10. The DAO layer
docs.text: One class per table. All follow the model from Example 28: an injected [Repository] [TypeORM], a [repo(manager)] method that selects the repository for the current transaction, and short methods with no business logic.

docs.title: 11.10.1. src/repositories/medecin.repository.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// repositories/medecin.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// DAO layer of the [Medecin] entity. Compared to the JSON server, three
// new features, all related to physician management by ADMIN:
//    - queries now also return the associated user account (relation
//      [user]), to display the login in the list of doctors;
//    - save() / deleteById(): create, update, delete;
//    - each write method accepts a EntityManager FACULTATIF: when
//      the business layer provides it, the operation is executed within the transaction
//      of that layer (see metier.service.ts, dataSource.transaction(...)).
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Medecin } from '../entities/medecin.entity';

@Injectable()
export class MedecinRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Medecin)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Medecin>,
  ) {}

   // the Repository to use: the one for the current transaction, if there is one
   // one; otherwise, the “standard” repository.
  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<Medecin> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(Medecin) : this.repository;
  }

   // list sorted by last name then first name, including the user account
  findAll(): Promise<Medecin[]> {
    return this.repository.find({ relations: { user: true }, order: { nom: 'ASC', prenom: 'ASC' } });
  }

  findById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Medecin | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { user: true } });
  }

   // the person with that first and last name, if there is one. The comparison
   // is performed by MySQL, using the database’s collation (utf8mb4_unicode_ci:
   // without taking case or accents into account)—exactly the same
   // rule as that of the uniqueness constraint SQL.
  findByPrenomNom(prenom: string, nom: string, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Medecin | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ prenom, nom });
  }

  save(medecin: Medecin, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Medecin> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(medecin);
  }

  async deleteById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete(id);
  }
}
  • lines 28–30: within a transaction, the repository for the current transaction ([manager]);
  • lines 33–35: all doctors, along with their account ([relations: { user: true }]), sorted by last name then first name. The account is used to display the login in the list of doctors;
  • lines 45–47: any potential namesakes. The comparison is performed by [MySQL], according to the database’s collation;
  • lines 49–51 and 53–55: write and delete operations.

docs.title: 11.10.2. src/repositories/client.repository.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// repositories/client.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// DAO layer of the [Client] entity (a PATIENT from the firm). Strictly
// the same principle as medecin.repository.ts (see its comments).
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Client } from '../entities/client.entity';

@Injectable()
export class ClientRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Client)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Client>,
  ) {}

  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<Client> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(Client) : this.repository;
  }

  findAll(): Promise<Client[]> {
    return this.repository.find({ relations: { user: true }, order: { nom: 'ASC', prenom: 'ASC' } });
  }

  findById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Client | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { user: true } });
  }

   // the client (patient) whose user account is [idUser], or null.
   // where: { user: { id } }: TypeORM translates this filter on the relation to
   // a simple "WHERE clients.user = ?" (no join required)
  findByUserId(idUser: number): Promise<Client | null> {
    return this.repository.findOne({ where: { user: { id: idUser } }, relations: { user: true } });
  }

   // reads a client by placing a VERROU on its line until the end of the
   // current transaction (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). A second transaction that
   // requires the same lock ATTEND until the first one is complete.
   // Used for scheduling appointments (see MetierService.ajouterRv): two
   // simultaneous appointments for the same patient are thus processed—one
   // APRÈS the other, and the second reservation reflects the appointment created by the first.
  verrouiller(id: number, manager: EntityManager): Promise<Client | null> {
    return manager.getRepository(Client).findOne({ where: { id }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } });
  }

   // the person with that first and last name, if there is one. The comparison
   // is performed by MySQL, using the database’s collation (utf8mb4_unicode_ci:
   // without taking case or accents into account)—exactly the same
   // rule as that of the uniqueness constraint SQL.
  findByPrenomNom(prenom: string, nom: string, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Client | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ prenom, nom });
  }

  save(client: Client, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Client> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(client);
  }

  async deleteById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete(id);
  }
}

The same methods as for doctors, plus two:

  • lines 35–37: the client whose account is specified—this is how a logged-in patient (whose token contains their account ID) retrieves their client record. [TypeORM] translates the filter [where: { user: { id: idUser } }] into [WHERE clients.user = ?];
  • lines 45–47: a read with a lock ([lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' }], i.e., [SELECT ... FOR UPDATE] in SQL). Until the end of the transaction, any other transaction requesting the same lock waits. The appointment scheduling module uses this to process two simultaneous reservations for the same patient one after the other.

// =========================================================================
// repositories/creneau.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Layer DAO of entity [Creneau]. New: deleteByMedecin(), used
// when deleting a doctor (their time slots disappear
// along with the doctor—see MetierService.supprimerMedecin).
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Creneau } from '../entities/creneau.entity';

@Injectable()
export class CreneauRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Creneau)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Creneau>,
  ) {}

  findById(id: number): Promise<Creneau | null> {
    return this.repository.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { medecin: true } });
  }

   // a doctor’s time slots, in chronological order
   // (same query as on the JSON server—see its comments)
  getAllCreneaux(idMedecin: number): Promise<Creneau[]> {
    return this.repository
      .createQueryBuilder('c')
      .where('c.medecin = :idMedecin', { idMedecin })
      .orderBy('c.hdebut', 'ASC')
      .addOrderBy('c.mdebut', 'ASC')
      .getMany();
  }

   // deletes all of a doctor’s appointment slots. delete({ doctor: { id } })
   // generates: DELETE FROM appointment slots WHERE id_medecin = ?
  async deleteByMedecin(idMedecin: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    const repo = manager ? manager.getRepository(Creneau) : this.repository;
    await repo.delete({ medecin: { id: idMedecin } });
  }
}
  • Lines 27–34: A doctor’s appointment slots, in chronological order. The query is written using QueryBuilder from [TypeORM], which constructs a SQL query method by method: [createQueryBuilder('c')] (the table, with the alias [c]), [where] (with a parameter named [:idMedecin]—never a string concatenation, which would open the door to SQL injections), [orderBy], then [getMany], which executes the query;
  • lines 38–41: Deleting a doctor’s appointment slots, used when that doctor is removed.

docs.title: 11.10.4. src/repositories/rv.repository.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// repositories/rv.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Layer DAO of the entity [Rv] (an appointment). New features:
//    - the number of appointments for a doctor, for REFUSER the removal
//      of a doctor who still has appointments (see MetierService);
//    - a patient’s appointments (the patient’s “My Account” page, and
//      rule: “only one upcoming appointment per patient”);
//    - Deletion of all appointments for a client (a client is
//      deleted along with their appointments, either by the ADMIN or by the client themselves).
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Rv } from '../entities/rv.entity';

@Injectable()
export class RvRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Rv)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Rv>,
  ) {}

  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<Rv> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(Rv) : this.repository;
  }

  findById(id: number): Promise<Rv | null> {
    return this.repository.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { client: true, creneau: true } });
  }

  save(rv: Rv, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Rv> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(rv);
  }

  async deleteById(id: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.repository.delete(id);
  }

   // a doctor’s appointments on a given day, including the client and time slot
   // (same query as on the JSON server—see its comments)
  getRvMedecinJour(idMedecin: number, jour: string): Promise<Rv[]> {
    return this.repository
      .createQueryBuilder('rv')
      .leftJoinAndSelect('rv.client', 'client')
      .leftJoinAndSelect('rv.creneau', 'creneau')
      .where('creneau.medecin = :idMedecin', { idMedecin })
      .andWhere('rv.jour = :jour', { jour })
      .getMany();
  }

   // a client's appointments starting from and including the day [depuis], in
   // chronological order, with the time slot ET and the doctor assigned to that time slot
   // (innerJoinAndSelect in cascade: appointment -> time slot -> doctor)
  findAVenirByClient(idClient: number, depuis: string): Promise<Rv[]> {
    return this.repository
      .createQueryBuilder('rv')
      .innerJoinAndSelect('rv.creneau', 'creneau')
      .innerJoinAndSelect('creneau.medecin', 'medecin')
      .where('rv.client = :idClient', { idClient })
      .andWhere('rv.jour >= :depuis', { depuis })
      .orderBy('rv.jour', 'ASC')
      .addOrderBy('creneau.hdebut', 'ASC')
      .addOrderBy('creneau.mdebut', 'ASC')
      .getMany();
  }

   // number of appointments for a client starting from day [depuis] (inclusive)
  countAVenirByClient(idClient: number, depuis: string, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<number> {
    return this.repo(manager)
      .createQueryBuilder('rv')
      .where('rv.client = :idClient', { idClient })
      .andWhere('rv.jour >= :depuis', { depuis })
      .getCount();
  }

   // deletes TOUS a client’s appointments (past and future):
   /  / DELETE FROM rv WHERE id_client = ?
  async deleteByClient(idClient: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete({ client: { id: idClient } });
  }

   // number of appointments (past or future) for a doctor—you must sort
   // through their time slots, since [rv] does not directly reference [medecins]:
   /  / SELECT COUNT(*) FROM rv INNER JOIN slots c ON ... WHERE c.id_medecin = ?
  countByMedecin(idMedecin: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<number> {
    return this.repo(manager)
      .createQueryBuilder('rv')
      .innerJoin('rv.creneau', 'creneau')
      .where('creneau.medecin = :idMedecin', { idMedecin })
      .getCount();
  }
}
  • lines 43–51: a doctor’s appointments for a given day. [leftJoinAndSelect] performs a join and loads the joined entity: each appointment is retrieved along with its patient and time slot;
  • lines 56–67: a client’s appointments starting on a given day, with their time slot and the doctor assigned to that slot (two cascading joins): this is what is displayed in “My Account”;
  • lines 70–76: their count, for the “only one upcoming appointment” rule;
  • lines 80–82: the deletion of all appointments for a client;
  • lines 87–93: the number of appointments for a doctor. The table [rv] does not directly reference doctors: you must go through the time slots ([innerJoin], a join without loading).

// =========================================================================
// repositories/user.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Layer DAO of entity [User]. New: save() / deleteById(), because
// creating (or deleting) a doctor or a client also creates (or deletes) their
// user account—see MetierService.
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { User } from '../entities/user.entity';

@Injectable()
export class UserRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(User)
    private readonly repository: Repository<User>,
  ) {}

  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<User> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(User) : this.repository;
  }

   // returns null if no user has that login
  findByLogin(login: string, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<User | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ login });
  }

  save(user: User, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<User> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(user);
  }

  async deleteById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete(id);
  }
}

Lines 26–28: a login’s account, used for logging in and to check if a login is available.

// =========================================================================
// job title/dates.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Today's date in "yyyy-MM-dd" format (the same as in the rv.jour column).
// It is used for RÈGLES, DE, and GESTION (no past appointments;
// a single appointment at VENIR per patient): it therefore resides in the
// business layer. The web layer reuses it (see web/helpers/dates.helper.ts).
//
// Two “yyyy-MM-dd” dates are compared directly as strings:
// "2026-09-23" < "2026-10-01"—alphabetical order is chronological order.
// =========================================================================

// Today’s date, in the server’s time zone
export function aujourdhui(): string {
  const d = new Date();
  const deuxChiffres = (n: number) => n.toString().padStart(2, '0');
  return `${d.getFullYear()}-${deuxChiffres(d.getMonth() + 1)}-${deuxChiffres(d.getDate())}`;
}

Lines 14–18: Today’s date in the format [aaaa-mm-jj]; the date in column [rv.jour]. [padStart(2, '0')] is used to pad a two-digit number (9 becomes [09]). In this format, alphabetical order is chronological order: two dates are compared using [<].

// =========================================================================
// business/metier.exception.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The exception thrown by the business layer when a RÈGLE DE GESTION is
// violated (username already taken, doctor still has appointments, time slot
// already reserved...). It does not carry text, but a CLÉ of
// translation (e.g., 'ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN'): it is the web layer that
// will translate into French or English when the page is displayed
// (see i18n/fr.json, i18n/en.json).
//
// The business layer thus remains independent of the interface language—
// just as it was already independent of the output format (JSON or HTML).
// =========================================================================

export class MetierException extends Error {
  constructor(
    public readonly cle: string, // message translation key
    public readonly params: Record<string, string> = {}, // any message parameters
  ) {
    super(cle);
    this.name = 'MetierException';
  }
}
  • line 17: a [MetierException] does not carry a message, but a translation key ([ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN]). The business layer thus ignores the interface language: the view will translate the key (see Chapter 5);
  • line 18: any message parameters;
  • line 21: the exception name, displayed in error logs.
