Content-Length: 79

{"message":"Cette ressource n'existe pas","error":"Not Found","statusCode":404}

In a browser, the difference between [text/html] and [text/plain] is visible:

docs.title: 2.4. Example 04: Redirects
docs.text:
An action may respond with a redirect: a 301 or 302 status code and a [Location] header that tells the browser which URL to request next. The browser requests it immediately, without user intervention. Redirects are ubiquitous in a web application: after a successful form submission, after logging in, after changing the language...

The [src/redirections.controller.ts] file:

import { Controller, Get, Param, Redirect } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller()
export class RedirectionsController {
   // fixed redirection: the URL and code are known in advance
  @Get('ancienne')
  @Redirect('/nouvelle', 301)
  ancienne(): void {}

  @Get('nouvelle')
  nouvelle(): string {
    return 'Vous êtes sur la page [nouvelle]';
  }

   // calculated redirection: the rendered object replaces the address of @Redirect()
  @Get('aller/:destination')
  @Redirect()
  aller(@Param('destination') destination: string): { url: string } {
    return { url: `/page/${destination}` };
  }

  @Get('page/:nom')
  page(@Param('nom') nom: string): string {
    return `Vous êtes sur la page [${nom}]`;
  }

   // redirect to another site
  @Get('documentation')
  @Redirect('https://docs.nestjs.com')
  documentation(): void {}
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • lines 6–8: [@Redirect('/nouvelle', 301)]: a permanent redirect. The 301 code (Moved Permanently) indicates that the page has permanently changed its address; the default code is 302 (Found), a temporary redirect;
  • lines 16–20: a calculated redirect: [@Redirect()] without an argument, and the action returns an object [{ url: ... }] that sets the destination address;
  • lines 28–30: You can redirect to another site.

[curl] shows the redirect without following it:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/old

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: /nouvelle
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 43

Moved Permanently. Redirecting to /nouvelle

With the [-L] option, [curl] follows the redirect, just as a browser would. We then see the two successive responses:

curl -i -L http://localhost:3000/old

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: /nouvelle
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Vous êtes sur la page [nouvelle]

curl -i http://localhost:3000/go/contact

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /page/contact
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 35

Found. Redirecting to /page/contact

In the browser, only the final page is visible; the address bar displays the new URL:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/documentation

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://docs.nestjs.com
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 45

Found. Redirecting to https://docs.nestjs.com

docs.title: 2.5. Example 05: The Request and Response Objects in Express
docs.text:
[NestJS] relies on the web server [Express]. An action can directly access the [Request] and [Response] objects from [Express]. This is sometimes necessary, and we’ll do it in the case study (to set a cookie, for example), but you need to be aware of what you’re losing.

The [src/express.controller.ts] file:

import { Controller, Get, Req, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';

@Controller('express')
export class ExpressController {
   // The Express request: method, URL, headers...
  @Get('requete')
  requete(@Req() req: Request): object {
    return {
      methode: req.method,
      url: req.url,
      chemin: req.path,
      navigateur: req.get('user-agent'),
    };
  }

   // the Express response: the action itself sends the response
  @Get('reponse')
  reponse(@Res() res: Response): void {
    res.status(200).type('text/plain').send('Réponse envoyée par [res.send]');
  }

   // redirection with the Express response
  @Get('redirection')
  redirection(@Res() res: Response): void {
    res.redirect('/express/reponse');
  }

   // passthrough: the response is used (here for a header), but NestJS
   // always sends the value returned by the action itself
  @Get('passthrough')
  passthrough(@Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response): string {
    res.setHeader('X-Exemple', '05-express');
    return 'Réponse envoyée par NestJS, avec un entête ajouté';
  }

   // ERREUR—do not do this: @Res() without passthrough, and nothing is sent
  @Get('bloquee')
  bloquee(@Res() res: Response): string {
    return 'Cette chaîne ne sera jamais envoyée : le navigateur attend...';
  }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 2: the types [Request] and [Response] from [Express];
  • Lines 7–15: [@Req()] injects the request [Express]: method HTTP, URL, path, headers ([req.get(...)])... ;
  • lines 18–21: [@Res()] injects the response [Express]. Note: As soon as an action uses [@Res()], [NestJS] assumes that it is the one sending the response and ignores what it returns. Here, the action sets the status code and type, and sends the body using [res.send];
  • lines 24–27: a 302 redirect performed by [Express] to [res.redirect(url)];
  • lines 31–35: With the [passthrough: true] option, the action uses the response (here to add a header) but lets [NestJS] send what it returns. It’s the best of both worlds;
  • lines 38–41: the mistake to avoid: [@Res()] without [passthrough], and no calls to [res.send], [res.redirect], [res.render].... The returned string is ignored, no response is ever sent, and the browser waits indefinitely.

Responses received:

curl -i -A "Mozilla/5.0 (exemple)" http://localhost:3000/express/request

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 107

{"methode":"GET","url":"/express/requete","chemin":"/express/requete","navigateur":"Mozilla/5.0 (exemple)"}

(the [-A] option in [curl] sets the [User-Agent] header, which identifies the browser)

curl -i http://localhost:3000/express/response

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 32

Réponse envoyée par [res.send]

curl -i http://localhost:3000/express/redirection

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /express/reponse
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 38

Found. Redirecting to /express/reponse

curl -i http://localhost:3000/express/passthrough

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Exemple: 05-express
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 53

Réponse envoyée par NestJS, avec un entête ajouté

For the last action, we limit the wait to 3 seconds using the [-m 3] option:

curl -i -m 3 http://localhost:3000/express/blocked

curl: (28) Operation timed out after 3002 milliseconds with 0 bytes received

In the rest of this document, we will use [@Res()] when an action must choose between several responses of different types (a page or a redirect), and we will ensure that each path in the code sends a response.

docs.title: 2.6. Example 06: Modules, Services, and Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Controllers should not contain application logic; they delegate it to services. Example 06 breaks down a small application into two modules:

06-modules/
├── src/
│   ├── clients/
│   │   ├── clients.controller.ts
│   │   └── clients.module.ts
│   ├── produits/
│   │   ├── produits.controller.ts
│   │   ├── produits.module.ts
│   │   └── produits.service.ts
│   ├── app.module.ts
│   └── main.ts
├── nest-cli.json
└── tsconfig.json

docs.title: 2.6.1. The ProduitsService service
docs.text:
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

export interface Produit {
  id: number;
  nom: string;
  prix: number;
}

@Injectable()
export class ProduitsService {
  private readonly produits: Produit[] = [
    { id: 1, nom: 'stylo', prix: 1.5 },
    { id: 2, nom: 'cahier', prix: 3.2 },
    { id: 3, nom: 'gomme', prix: 0.8 },
  ];

  findAll(): Produit[] {
    return this.produits;
  }

  findById(id: number): Produit | undefined {
    return this.produits.find((p) => p.id === id);
  }
}
  • Lines 3–7: The [Produit] interface describes a product;
  • line 9: the decorator [@Injectable()] turns the class into a service (also called a provider): [NestJS] creates a single instance of it, which it provides (injects) to all who need it;
  • lines 11–15: the data, here in memory;
  • lines 17–23: the service’s two methods.

docs.title: 2.6.2. The ProduitsController controller
docs.text:
import { Controller, Get, NotFoundException, Param } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Produit, ProduitsService } from './produits.service';

@Controller('produits')
export class ProduitsController {
   // dependency injection: NestJS provides the instance of ProduitsService
  constructor(private readonly produitsService: ProduitsService) {}

  @Get()
  liste(): Produit[] {
    return this.produitsService.findAll();
  }

  @Get(':id')
  unProduit(@Param('id') id: string): Produit {
    const produit = this.produitsService.findById(Number(id));
    if (!produit) {
      throw new NotFoundException(`Produit n° ${id} introuvable`);
    }
    return produit;
  }
}
  • line 7: dependency injection. The controller declares in its constructor that it needs a [ProduitsService]; [NestJS] provides it with the single instance of the service. The controller never calls [new ProduitsService()]. The syntax [private readonly produitsService: ProduitsService] of [TypeScript] declares both the parameter and the field [this.produitsService];
  • Lines 9–12: The action delegates to the service;
  • lines 14–21: [Number(id)] converts the route parameter (a string) into a number. A non-existent product triggers a 404 exception.

docs.title: 2.6.3. The ProduitsModule module
docs.text:
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ProduitsController } from './produits.controller';
import { ProduitsService } from './produits.service';

@Module({
  controllers: [ProduitsController],
  providers: [ProduitsService],
  exports: [ProduitsService],
})
export class ProduitsModule {}
  • line 6: the module’s controller;
  • line 7: the module’s services. Only the services declared here (or imported, see below) can be injected into the module’s classes;
  • line 8: the service is exported: modules that import [ProduitsModule] will also be able to have it injected.

docs.title: 2.6.4. The ClientsModule module
docs.text:
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ClientsController } from './clients.controller';
import { ProduitsModule } from '../produits/produits.module';

@Module({
  imports: [ProduitsModule],
  controllers: [ClientsController],
})
export class ClientsModule {}

Line 6: [ClientsModule] imports [ProduitsModule] and therefore has access to the services that the latter exports.

The file [src/clients/clients.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ProduitsService } from '../produits/produits.service';

@Controller('clients')
export class ClientsController {
   // a service from a AUTRE module, exported by that module
  constructor(private readonly produitsService: ProduitsService) {}

  @Get('panier')
  panier(): object {
    const produits = this.produitsService.findAll();
    const total = produits.reduce((somme, p) => somme + p.prix, 0);
    return { client: 'Jean Martin', articles: produits.length, total };
  }
}
  • Line 7: [ClientsController] has a service from another module injected into it;
  • lines 9–14: it uses this service to calculate the total of a shopping cart.

docs.title: 2.6.5. The root module
docs.text:
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ProduitsModule } from './produits/produits.module';
import { ClientsModule } from './clients/clients.module';

@Module({
  imports: [ProduitsModule, ClientsModule],
})
export class AppModule {}

line 6: the root module no longer has a controller; it simply imports the application’s two modules.

docs.title: 6. Data Scopes
docs.text:
A web application serves many users at once, and each user makes numerous requests. Data can therefore be shared at three levels, known as its scope:

  • application scope: the data is shared by all users throughout the server’s lifetime (the list of doctors, for example);
  • request scope: the data exists only for the duration of a request (a view’s model);
  • client scope: the data is specific to a user and must persist from one request to the next (the selected language, the logged-in user).

The original course used the [ASP.NET] session for this last scope: a server-side storage space unique to each browser. This document, like the case study, does without it: client-side scope data is stored by the browser in cookies. The server does not store anything between two requests from the same user: it is said to be stateless ([stateless]). This is what makes it possible, for example, to run multiple identical servers behind a load balancer. The trade-off: a cookie is under the user’s control, and the user can read and modify it. Chapter 8 will show how a signed token makes it possible to trust the cookie despite this.

docs.title: 6.1. Example 23: Three Scopes
docs.text:
The file [src/compteur.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

// scope APPLICATION (the default): a single instance, created at startup and
// shared by TOUTES; requests from TOUS; users
@Injectable()
export class CompteurService {
  private total = 0;

  incrementer(): number {
    return ++this.total;
  }
}

Lines 5–6: By default, a [NestJS] service is a singleton: a single instance, created at startup, shared by all requests. Its [total] field therefore has application scope.

The [src/requete.service.ts] file:

import { Injectable, Scope } from '@nestjs/common';

let instancesCreees = 0;

// scope REQUÊTE: one NOUVELLE instance for each HTTP request
@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })
export class RequeteService {
  readonly numero = ++instancesCreees;
}

Line 6: The [scope: Scope.REQUEST] option requests a new instance for each request. The instance number indicates this. This option is rarely used: it incurs a cost (creating objects for each request), and it propagates—a controller that depends on a request-scope service becomes request-scope itself. [res.locals] is usually sufficient.

The file [src/portees.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get, Req, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { CompteurService } from './compteur.service';
import { RequeteService } from './requete.service';

@Controller()
export class PorteesController {
  constructor(
    private readonly compteur: CompteurService,
    private readonly requete: RequeteService,
  ) {}

  @Get()
  portees(@Req() req: Request, @Res() res: Response): void {
     // scope CLIENT: data stored by NAVIGATEUR (cookie),
     // sent back to the server with each request
    const mesVisites = Number(req.cookies?.mesVisites ?? 0) + 1;
    res.cookie('mesVisites', String(mesVisites), { httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' });
    res.render('portees', {
      total: this.compteur.incrementer(),
      instance: this.requete.numero,
      mesVisites,
    });
  }
}
  • lines 8–11: both services are injected;
  • lines 17–18: the client scope: a counter stored in a cookie. The browser sends it back with every request; the action increments it and stores it back;
  • lines 19–23: the three values are passed to the view.

The file [src/main.ts]:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import * as cookieParser from 'cookie-parser';
import { NextFunction, Request, Response } from 'express';
import { dirname, join } from 'path';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);
  app.useStaticAssets(join(dirname(require.resolve('bootstrap/package.json')), 'dist'), { prefix: '/bootstrap/' });
  app.setBaseViewsDir(join(__dirname, '..', 'views'));
  app.setViewEngine('hbs');
  app.use(cookieParser());
   // scope REQUÊTE: res.locals is created and deleted with the request
  app.use((req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
    res.locals.debut = new Date().toISOString().slice(11, 23);
    next();
  });
  await app.listen(3000);
  console.log('Serveur démarré sur http://localhost:3000');
}

bootstrap();

lines 15–18: the request scope with [res.locals]: the time the request was received.

The file [views/portees.hbs]:

<h1 class="h3">Les portées des données</h1>
<ul>
  <li>application : {{total}} visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
  <li>requête : instance n° {{instance}} de RequeteService, requête reçue à {{debut}}</li>
  <li>client : {{mesVisites}} visite(s) de ce navigateur</li>
</ul>

Let’s simulate two browsers with [curl] and two cookie files, [a.txt] and [b.txt]. Browser A makes two requests, then browser B makes one, and finally A makes one more:

curl -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:3000/
curl -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:3000/
curl -c b.txt -b b.txt http://localhost:3000/
curl -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:3000/

navigateur A :
application : 1 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus
requête : instance n° 1 de RequeteService, requête reçue à 14:16:07.195
client : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur

navigateur A :
application : 2 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus
requête : instance n° 2 de RequeteService, requête reçue à 14:16:07.237
client : 2 visite(s) de ce navigateur

navigateur B :
application : 3 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus
requête : instance n° 3 de RequeteService, requête reçue à 14:16:07.251
client : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur

navigateur A :
application : 4 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus
requête : instance n° 4 de RequeteService, requête reçue à 14:16:07.263
client : 3 visite(s) de ce navigateur
  • The application counter counts all visits: 1, 2, 3, 4;
  • each request has its own instance of [RequeteService]: 1, 2, 3, 4;
  • The client counter is specific to each browser: A has 3 visits, B has 1.

docs.title: 5. Internationalization
docs.text: An internationalized application displays its text in the user’s language. The case study is in French and English. The principle is simple: the views no longer contain text, but keys ([MENU.ACCUEIL]), and a dictionary for each language associates a text with each key. The selected language is stored in a cookie.

docs.title: 5.1.1. The Dictionaries
docs.text:
The file [i18n/fr.json]:

{
  "MENU": {
    "ACCUEIL": "Accueil",
    "PRODUITS": "Produits"
  },
  "ACCUEIL": {
    "TITRE": "Bienvenue",
    "BONJOUR": "Bonjour {nom} !",
    "DATE": "Nous sommes le {date}."
  },
  "PRODUITS": {
    "TITRE": "Nos produits",
    "NOM": "Produit",
    "PRIX": "Prix",
    "NOMBRE": "{n} produit(s) au catalogue."
  }
}

The file [i18n/en.json]:

{
  "MENU": {
    "ACCUEIL": "Home",
    "PRODUITS": "Products"
  },
  "ACCUEIL": {
    "TITRE": "Welcome",
    "BONJOUR": "Hello {nom}!",
    "DATE": "Today is {date}."
  },
  "PRODUITS": {
    "TITRE": "Our products",
    "NOM": "Product",
    "PRIX": "Price",
    "NOMBRE": "{n} product(s) in the catalogue."
  }
}
  • A dictionary is a JSON file, organized by page or by topic: The key [ACCUEIL.BONJOUR] refers to the text [BONJOUR] in section [ACCUEIL];
  • Line 8: A text may contain parameters, enclosed in curly braces, which are replaced during translation. Word order varies from one language to another: this is why a text is not created by simply concatenating translated segments.

docs.title: 5.1.2. The translation module
docs.text:
The file [src/i18n.ts]:

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { join } from 'path';

export type Langue = 'fr' | 'en';
export const LANGUES: Langue[] = ['fr', 'en'];
export const LANGUE_PAR_DEFAUT: Langue = 'fr';
// the "locale" used by Intl for dates and numbers
export const LOCALES: Record<Langue, string> = { fr: 'fr-FR', en: 'en-US' };

// A dictionary is a nested JSON object: { "MENU": { "ACCUEIL": "Home" } }
type Dictionnaire = { [cle: string]: string | Dictionnaire };

// Dictionaries are read UNE times at startup
const DOSSIER = join(__dirname, '..', 'i18n');
const dictionnaires: Record<Langue, Dictionnaire> = {
  fr: JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(DOSSIER, 'fr.json'), 'utf-8')),
  en: JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(DOSSIER, 'en.json'), 'utf-8')),
};

export function estUneLangue(valeur: unknown): valeur is Langue {
  return typeof valeur === 'string' && (LANGUES as string[]).includes(valeur);
}

// translate('fr', 'ACCUEIL.BONJOUR', { name: 'Marie' }) -> "Hello Marie!"
export function traduire(langue: Langue, cle: string, params: Record<string, unknown> = {}): string {
  const texte = chercher(dictionnaires[langue], cle) ?? cle;
  return texte.replace(/\{(\w+)\}/g, (tout, nom: string) => (nom in params ? String(params[nom]) : tout));
}

// 'ACCUEIL.BONJOUR': we go down to ACCUEIL, then to BONJOUR
function chercher(dictionnaire: Dictionnaire, cle: string): string | null {
  let noeud: string | Dictionnaire | undefined = dictionnaire;
  for (const morceau of cle.split('.')) {
    if (typeof noeud !== 'object') {
      return null;
    }
    noeud = noeud[morceau];
  }
  return typeof noeud === 'string' ? noeud : null;
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 4–6: the supported languages;
  • line 8: the “locale” for each language, used by [Intl] to format dates and numbers ([fr-FR]: 09/23/2026, €12.50; [en-US]: 9/23/2026, €12.50);
  • lines 14–18: the dictionaries are read once, when the module loads, and then kept in memory;
  • lines 20–22: a check for a type such as [TypeScript] ([valeur is Langue]): after a positive test, the compiler knows that the value is a [Langue];
  • lines 25–28: the translation. The key is looked up in the dictionary; if it is not found, the key itself is displayed: any omission is immediately visible on the screen. The regular expression [/\{(\w+)\}/g] finds each parameter [{nom}] and replaces it with its value;
  • lines 31–40: The key [ACCUEIL.BONJOUR] is split into [ACCUEIL] and then [BONJOUR], and the process continues down into the object JSON.

docs.title: 5.1.3. The helpers
docs.text:
The file [src/helpers.ts]:

import { HelperOptions } from 'handlebars';
import { Langue, LANGUE_PAR_DEFAUT, LOCALES, estUneLangue, traduire } from './i18n';

interface Hbs {
  registerHelper(nom: string, fonction: (...args: any[]) => unknown): void;
}

// the page's language: res.locals.lang, merged into the root template
function langueDe(options: HelperOptions): Langue {
  const lang = options.data?.root?.lang;
  return estUneLangue(lang) ? lang : LANGUE_PAR_DEFAUT;
}

export function enregistrerHelpers(hbs: Hbs): void {
   // {{t 'CLE'}} or {{t 'CLE' name=...}}: translation, with named parameters
  hbs.registerHelper('t', (cle: string, options: HelperOptions) => traduire(langueDe(options), cle, options.hash));

   // {{dateLongue when}}: "Wednesday, September 23, 2026" / "Wednesday, September 23, 2026"
  hbs.registerHelper('dateLongue', (quand: string, options: HelperOptions) =>
    new Intl.DateTimeFormat(LOCALES[langueDe(options)], { dateStyle: 'full' }).format(new Date(quand)),
  );

   // {{currency price}}: "12.50 €" / "€12.50"
  hbs.registerHelper('monnaie', (montant: number, options: HelperOptions) =>
    new Intl.NumberFormat(LOCALES[langueDe(options)], { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(montant),
  );

  hbs.registerHelper('eq', (a: unknown, b: unknown) => a === b);
}
  • lines 9–12: The page’s language is in the root template ([options.data.root.lang]), where the [main.ts] middleware placed it via [res.locals];
  • line 16: the helper [t] translates a key. The named parameters of the helper ([options.hash]) are the text parameters: [{{t 'ACCUEIL.BONJOUR' nom=nom}}];
  • lines 19–21 and 24–26: dates and amounts are formatted according to the language.

docs.title: 5.1.4. Language Selection
docs.text:
The file [src/main.ts]:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import * as cookieParser from 'cookie-parser';
import { NextFunction, Request, Response } from 'express';
import * as hbs from 'hbs';
import { dirname, join } from 'path';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { enregistrerHelpers } from './helpers';
import { estUneLangue, LANGUE_PAR_DEFAUT } from './i18n';

const RACINE = join(__dirname, '..');

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);
  app.useStaticAssets(join(dirname(require.resolve('bootstrap/package.json')), 'dist'), { prefix: '/bootstrap/' });
  app.setBaseViewsDir(join(RACINE, 'views'));
  app.setViewEngine('hbs');
  enregistrerHelpers(hbs);
  await new Promise<void>((fini) => hbs.registerPartials(join(RACINE, 'views', 'partials'), () => fini()));
  app.use(cookieParser());
   // the language of each page: the language specified in the [langue] cookie, or French otherwise
  app.use((req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
    const cookie = req.cookies?.langue;
    res.locals.lang = estUneLangue(cookie) ? cookie : LANGUE_PAR_DEFAUT;
    next();
  });
  await app.listen(3000);
  console.log('Serveur démarré sur http://localhost:3000');
}

bootstrap();

Lines 22–26: For each request, the language is read from the [langue] cookie (French by default) and stored in [res.locals.lang], and thus in the template for each view.

The file [src/langue.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get, NotFoundException, Param, Req, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { estUneLangue } from './i18n';

@Controller('langue')
export class LangueController {
   // GET /language/en: saves the selection in a cookie, then returns to the previous page
  @Get(':langue')
  changer(@Param('langue') langue: string, @Req() req: Request, @Res() res: Response): void {
    if (!estUneLangue(langue)) {
      throw new NotFoundException();
    }
    res.cookie('langue', langue, { maxAge: 365 * 24 * 3600 * 1000, sameSite: 'lax', httpOnly: true });
    res.redirect(pageDOrigine(req));
  }
}

// the page you came from (Referer header), of which only the path is retained:
// Redirecting to a full URL from the request would allow
// to send the user to another site (“open redirect” vulnerability)
function pageDOrigine(req: Request): string {
  const referer = req.get('referer');
  if (!referer) {
    return '/';
  }
  try {
    const url = new URL(referer);
    return url.pathname + url.search;
  } catch {
    return '/';
  }
}
  • lines 8–15: [GET /langue/en] stores the selection in a cookie valid for one year, then redirects to the page the user came from. An unknown language results in a 404 error;
  • lines 21–32: The original page is specified by the [Referer] header, which the browser adds when a link is clicked. We retain only the path: redirecting to a full URL from the request would allow a malicious site to create a link that, after passing through our site, sends the user to the malicious site (a vulnerability known as [open redirect]).

docs.text:
The [views/layout.hbs] file:

<!doctype html>

The file [views/partials/navbar.hbs]:

<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">

The file [views/accueil.hbs]:

<h1>{{t 'ACCUEIL.TITRE'}}</h1>
<p>{{t 'ACCUEIL.BONJOUR' nom=nom}}</p>

The [src/pages.controller.ts] file:

import { Controller, Get, Render } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller()
export class PagesController {
  @Get()
  @Render('accueil')
  accueil(): object {
     // titrePage is a CLÉ: the view translates it
    return { titrePage: 'ACCUEIL.TITRE', nom: 'Marie', aujourdhui: '2026-09-23' };
  }

  @Get('produits')
  @Render('produits')
  produits(): object {
    const produits = [
      { nom: 'Clavier', prix: 25 },
      { nom: 'Souris', prix: 12.5 },
      { nom: 'Écran', prix: 1149 },
    ];
    return { titrePage: 'PRODUITS.TITRE', produits, nombre: produits.length };
  }
}

docs.title: 5.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
In French (no cookie yet):

Click on EN:

curl -i -H "Referer: http://localhost:3000/produits" http://localhost:3000/language/en

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Set-Cookie: langue=en; Max-Age=31536000; Path=/; Expires=Thu, 23 Sep 2027 14:16:03 GMT; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Location: /produits
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 31

Found. Redirecting to /produits

The server sets the cookie and redirects to the original page, which is now in English:

The case study proceeds exactly this way, using more comprehensive dictionaries ([i18n/fr.json] and [i18n/en.json]): same helper [t], same controller [/langue/:langue], same cookie. There is only one difference: the error messages generated by the business and web layers are also keys, translated at the last moment by the view.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. Its purpose is to adapt the document *Introduction to ASP.NET MVC by Example* (2013) to the [NestJS] web framework:

  • the [ASP.NET MVC] framework and the [C#] language are replaced by the [NestJS] framework and the [TypeScript] language;
  • the [Razor] views are replaced by [Handlebars] views;
  • [Entity Framework] data access is replaced by ORM, [TypeORM], and a [MySQL] database.

The document follows the structure of the original course: first, numerous small projects, each focused on a single concept, followed by a comprehensive case study—a web application for scheduling appointments at a medical practice—with all files fully commented. The chapter from the original course devoted to the basics of web programming (the HTTP protocol, the HTML language) has not been included: these basics are assumed to be known.

docs.title: 1.1. The Role of NestJS in a Web Application
docs.text:
A web application is often built in layers, with each layer communicating only with its neighboring layers:

  • the web layer receives HTTP requests from the browser and returns HTML pages to it. [NestJS] helps us write this layer;
  • the business layer contains the application’s business rules (e.g., “a patient can have only one upcoming appointment”). It knows nothing about the web: it could just as easily serve a command-line application;
  • the data access layer (layer [DAO], for [Data Access Object]) reads from and writes to the database. We will use the ORM [TypeORM] ([Object Relational Mapper]), which maps the rows of the tables to the [TypeScript] objects.

The web layer itself follows the [MVC] ([Model – View – Controller]) model:

  • the controller (C) is a class whose methods—called actions—each handle a specific type of request (for example, [GET /agenda]). An action reads the request parameters, invokes the business layer, and then selects the view to display;
  • the model (M) is the set of data that the action passes to the view: a simple [JavaScript] object;
  • the view (V) is a [Handlebars] file (extension [.hbs]): a HTML file in which [{{...}}] tags are replaced by data from the model.

The processing of a request follows the numbered steps in the diagram:

  • 1: The browser sends a HTTP request, for example, [GET /agenda?idMedecin=1&jour=2026-09-24];
  • 2: [NestJS], which relies on the web server [Express], selects the action responsible for handling this request: this is routing. Before reaching that point, the request may pass through middleware, guards, interceptors, and pipes, which we’ll explore in the following chapters;
  • 3: The action requests the data it needs from the business layer;
  • 4: It builds the view template and specifies the view that should display it;
  • 5: The [Handlebars] view engine generates the HTML page, which [NestJS] returns to the browser.

[NestJS] is a [Node.js] framework written in [TypeScript]. It builds on the concepts of the [Spring] ([Java]) and [Angular] frameworks: decorators ([@Controller], [@Get], [@Injectable]...) describe the role of each class, and dependency injection provides each object with the dependencies it needs. It is often used to write servers that return JSON to a client [JavaScript] ([Angular], [React], [Flutter]...). This document uses it to write a classic web application: the server generates the HTML pages, and the browser simply displays them.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • [Node.js] 20 and its package manager [npm];
  • the editor [Visual Studio Code];
  • a recent browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]);
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays raw HTTP responses (it is included with [Windows] 10 and 11);
  • the SGBD [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, the one for [Laragon] under [Windows], starting with the chapter on data access.

The library versions are those in the [package.json] file in the examples folder: [NestJS] 10, [TypeScript] 5, [hbs] 4 ([Handlebars]), [class-validator] 0.14, [TypeORM] 0.3, [Bootstrap] 5.

docs.title: 1.3. Examples
docs.text:
The examples are stored in a folder named [exemples], with one subfolder per example:

exemples/
├── 01-structure/
├── 02-routage/
├── ...
├── 28-couches/
├── node_modules/
├── package.json
└── package-lock.json

All examples share the same libraries, which are declared in [exemples/package.json]. They are installed once, in a console opened to the [exemples] folder. In VSCode, open the examples folder:

then, in a terminal integrated into VSCode, type the command

npm install

Each example then has the minimal structure of a [NestJS] project:

13-premiere-vue/
├── src/
│   ├── app.module.ts
│   ├── main.ts
│   └── vues.controller.ts
├── views/
│   ├── inconnu.hbs
│   └── index.hbs
├── nest-cli.json
└── tsconfig.json
  • [src]: the code [TypeScript];
  • [views]: the views from [Handlebars] (starting in Chapter 4);
  • [nest-cli.json]: the command-line tool configuration for [NestJS];
  • [tsconfig.json]: the configuration of the [TypeScript] compiler.

To run an example, open a console in the

and type:

npx nest start

[npx] locates the tool [nest] in the [node_modules] folder within the parent folder. [nest start] compiles the code [TypeScript] in the [dist] folder, then executes [dist/main.js]. With the [--watch] option, the code is recompiled and the server restarted whenever a [.ts] file is modified:

npx nest start --watch

All examples listen on port 3000: only one can be running at a time. Stop the server using [Ctrl-C] in the console.

The file [tsconfig.json] is the same for all examples:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "commonjs",
    "target": "ES2022",
    "lib": ["ES2022"],
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "./src",
    "sourceMap": true,
    "emitDecoratorMetadata": true,
    "experimentalDecorators": true,
    "allowSyntheticDefaultImports": true,
    "strictNullChecks": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

Let’s comment on this file:

  • line 3: the compiled code uses the modules [CommonJS] from [Node.js] ([require]);
  • line 4: the generated code is from the recent [JavaScript] (ES2022), which includes [Node.js] 20;
  • lines 6–7: the source code is in [src], and the compiled code is in [dist];
  • lines 9–10: required for [NestJS]. Decorators ([@Controller]...) are a feature of [TypeScript] that must be enabled, and [emitDecoratorMetadata] preserves the types of constructor and method parameters in the compiled code: it is thanks to this that [NestJS] knows which object to inject into a constructor;
  • Line 12: The compiler reports the use of a value that may be [null] or [undefined];
  • line 13: library declaration files are not checked (faster compilation).

The file [nest-cli.json] is also common to all examples:

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/nest-cli",
  "collection": "@nestjs/schematics",
  "sourceRoot": "src",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "deleteOutDir": true
  }
}
  • line 4: the source code is in [src];
  • line 6: the [dist] folder is emptied before each compilation (a file deleted from [src] does not leave behind an outdated compiled copy).

The document proceeds as follows:

Each example introduces only a few new concepts, and the chapters build on one another: it is best to read them in order. The case study, meanwhile, draws on all the concepts from the previous chapters: whenever relevant, its commentary refers to the example where the concept was introduced.

docs.title: 9. Layered Architecture and Data Access
docs.text:
The previous examples kept their data in memory. A real application stores it in a database and is organized into layers (see the diagram in the introduction):

  • the web layer (controllers, views): read the request, call the business layer, select the view;
  • the business layer: business rules;
  • the DAO layer: database queries.

Each layer is aware only of the layer below it, and as few details about it as possible: the web layer is unaware of the SQL layer, and the business layer is unaware of the HTML layer. This separation makes each layer easier to understand, test, and evolve. Example 28 applies this to managing a list of people: it is, on a smaller scale, the management of doctors and clients from the case study.

docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The database [dbpersonnes] is created by a script SQL. Using [Laragon], it can be run, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersonnes.sql

The [database/dbpersonnes.sql] file:

-- Based on Example 28: a single table, [personnes]
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersonnes;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersonnes CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersonnes;

CREATE TABLE personnes (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  prenom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  nom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
   -- Two people cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_personnes_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO personnes (prenom, nom, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The [utf8mb4] character set accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents: for MySQL, [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 8: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 14: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names. The name will be used to identify the error.

docs.title: 9.1.2. The configuration of TypeORM
docs.text:
The [src/config/database.config.ts] file:

import { TypeOrmModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Personne } from '../entities/personne.entity';

// Database connection; the default values are those of Laragon
export function configBase(): TypeOrmModuleOptions {
  return {
    type: 'mysql',
    host: process.env.DB_HOST ?? 'localhost',
    port: Number(process.env.DB_PORT ?? 3306),
    username: process.env.DB_USERNAME ?? 'root',
    password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD ?? '',
    database: 'dbpersonnes',
    entities: [Personne],
     // The schema is created by the script SQL and is never modified by TypeORM
    synchronize: false,
     // DB_LOGGING=true: displays the SQL commands sent to the database
    logging: process.env.DB_LOGGING === 'true',
  };
}
  • Lines 8–11: connection parameters, read from environment variables, with the default values from [Laragon] (username [root], no password);
  • line 13: the classes that [TypeORM] maps to tables;
  • line 15: [TypeORM] could create or modify the tables itself based on the classes. This is convenient for a prototype but dangerous for a database containing data: the schema remains the responsibility of the SQL script;
  • line 17: with the environment variable [DB_LOGGING=true], the SQL commands sent to the database are displayed in the console.

docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person entity
docs.text:
The file [src/entities/personne.entity.ts]:

import { Column, Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

// a row in the [personnes] table <-> a Person object
@Entity('personnes')
export class Personne {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn()
  id: number;

   // incremented by TypeORM with each modification (optimistic lock)
  @VersionColumn()
  version: number;

  @Column({ length: 30 })
  prenom: string;

  @Column({ length: 30 })
  nom: string;

  @Column()
  age: number;
}
  • Line 4: The class [Personne] corresponds to the table [personnes]: each row of the table will be a [Personne] object;
  • line 6: the primary key, generated by the database ([AUTO_INCREMENT]);
  • Line 10: the version column, managed by [TypeORM];
  • rows 13–20: the other columns.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer
docs.text:
The file [src/dao/personnes.dao.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Not, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Personne } from '../entities/personne.entity';

// the layer of ACCÈS AUX DONNÉES: queries, no business rules
@Injectable()
export class PersonnesDao {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Personne) private readonly repository: Repository<Personne>) {}

   // In a transaction, you must go through the transaction “manager”
  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<Personne> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(Personne) : this.repository;
  }

  lister(): Promise<Personne[]> {
    return this.repository.find({ order: { nom: 'ASC', prenom: 'ASC' } });
  }

  lire(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Personne | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ id });
  }

   // a person (with an ID different from [saufId]) with this first and last name
  homonyme(prenom: string, nom: string, saufId: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Personne | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ prenom, nom, id: Not(saufId) });
  }

   // INSERT if the person has no ID; otherwise, UPDATE
  sauvegarder(personne: Personne, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Personne> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(personne);
  }

  async supprimer(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete(id);
  }
}
  • line 9: [TypeORM] provides a repository ([Repository<Personne>]) for each entity that can read from and write to the table. [@InjectRepository] injects it;
  • lines 12–14: Within a transaction, all queries must go through the same [EntityManager] object—the one associated with the transaction. Each method therefore accepts an optional [manager];
  • lines 16–18: [find] with a sort: [SELECT ... ORDER BY nom, prenom];
  • lines 25–27: a person with the same first and last name, other than [saufId] ([Not]): useful for modifying a record, which must not conflict with itself;
  • lines 30–32: [save] becomes [INSERT] if the object has no identifier, and [UPDATE] otherwise.

The DAO layer contains no rules: only queries.

docs.title: 9.1.5. The business layer
docs.text:
The file [src/metier/metier.exception.ts]:

// A business rule rejects the operation: this is not an error,
// the message is intended for the user
export class MetierException extends Error {}

A [MetierException] indicates that a business rule has rejected an operation. This is not a program error: the message is intended for the user.

The [src/metier/personnes.metier.ts] file:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';
import { PersonnesDao } from '../dao/personnes.dao';
import { Personne } from '../entities/personne.entity';
import { MetierException } from './metier.exception';

export interface DonneesPersonne {
  prenom: string;
  nom: string;
  age: number;
}

// the MÉTIER layer: the business rules, and only those rules
@Injectable()
export class PersonnesMetier {
  constructor(
    private readonly dao: PersonnesDao,
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
  ) {}

  lister(): Promise<Personne[]> {
    return this.dao.lister();
  }

  async lire(id: number): Promise<Personne> {
    const personne = await this.dao.lire(id);
    if (!personne) {
      throw new MetierException("Cette personne n'existe pas (ou plus).");
    }
    return personne;
  }

  ajouter(donnees: DonneesPersonne): Promise<Personne> {
    return this.transaction(async (manager) => {
       // Rule 1: No two people can have the same first and last names
      if (await this.dao.homonyme(donnees.prenom, donnees.nom, 0, manager)) {
        throw new MetierException('Une personne porte déjà ces prénom et nom.');
      }
      const personne = new Personne();
      personne.prenom = donnees.prenom;
      personne.nom = donnees.nom;
      personne.age = donnees.age;
      return this.dao.sauvegarder(personne, manager);
    });
  }

  modifier(id: number, version: number, donnees: DonneesPersonne): Promise<Personne> {
    return this.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const personne = await this.dao.lire(id, manager);
      if (!personne) {
        throw new MetierException("Cette personne n'existe pas (ou plus).");
      }
       // Rule 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else
      if (personne.version !== version) {
        throw new MetierException('Cette fiche a été modifiée entre-temps : rechargez-la.');
      }
      if (await this.dao.homonyme(donnees.prenom, donnees.nom, id, manager)) {
        throw new MetierException('Une personne porte déjà ces prénom et nom.');
      }
      personne.prenom = donnees.prenom;
      personne.nom = donnees.nom;
      personne.age = donnees.age;
      return this.dao.sauvegarder(personne, manager);
    });
  }

  async supprimer(id: number): Promise<Personne> {
    const personne = await this.lire(id);
    await this.dao.supprimer(id);
    return personne;
  }

   // [travail] runs within a transaction: COMMIT if it succeeds, ROLLBACK
   // if it throws an exception. A violation of the uniqueness constraint (two
   // simultaneous insertions, for example) results in a MetierException
  private async transaction<R>(travail: (manager: EntityManager) => Promise<R>): Promise<R> {
    try {
      return await this.dataSource.transaction(travail);
    } catch (e) {
      const erreurSql = e as { code?: string; message?: string };
      if (erreurSql.code === 'ER_DUP_ENTRY' && erreurSql.message?.includes('unq_personnes_prenom_nom')) {
        throw new MetierException('Une personne porte déjà ces prénom et nom.');
      }
      throw e;
    }
  }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • lines 16–19: The business layer uses DAO, and [DataSource] from [TypeORM] (the database connection) to open transactions;
  • lines 25–31: an absent person is a [MetierException];
  • lines 33–45: adding a person within a transaction. Rule: no two people may have the same first and last names. This is verified before the write operation to display a clear message;
  • lines 47–65: modification. Additional rule: the optimistic lock (lines 54–56): the modification form carries the version of the record as it was when the form was opened. If it has changed in the meantime (another user has modified the same record), the operation is rejected rather than silently overwriting the user’s work;
  • lines 76–86: [dataSource.transaction(travail)] opens a transaction, executes [travail], then validates it ([COMMIT]) or rolls it back ([ROLLBACK]) if [travail] throws an exception. Lines 81–82: Preliminary checking for homonyms is not always sufficient: two users may add the same person at the same time, and both may pass the check. The database’s uniqueness constraint, however, does not allow any exceptions; the error MySQL [ER_DUP_ENTRY], identified by the constraint, then becomes the same [MetierException].

docs.title: 9.1.6. The Web Layer
docs.text:
The file [src/web/formulaire-personne.dto.ts]:

import { Transform, Type } from 'class-transformer';
import { IsInt, IsNotEmpty, Max, MaxLength, Min } from 'class-validator';

const nettoyer = ({ value }: { value: unknown }) => (typeof value === 'string' ? value.trim() : value);

// the form fields and their constraints (lengths = SQL columns)
export class FormulairePersonneDto {
  @Transform(nettoyer)
  @IsNotEmpty({ message: 'Le prénom est obligatoire.' })
  @MaxLength(30, { message: 'Le prénom ne doit pas dépasser 30 caractères.' })
  prenom: string;

  @Transform(nettoyer)
  @IsNotEmpty({ message: 'Le nom est obligatoire.' })
  @MaxLength(30, { message: 'Le nom ne doit pas dépasser 30 caractères.' })
  nom: string;

  @Type(() => Number)
  @IsInt({ message: "L'âge doit être un nombre entier." })
  @Min(0, { message: "L'âge doit être positif." })
  @Max(150, { message: "L'âge ne peut dépasser 150." })
  age: number;
}

The form and its constraints (see Example 19). The function [validerFormulaire] (file [web/validation.ts]) is the one from Example 19, and [web/flash.ts] is the one from Example 20, supplemented with a message type (success or error).

The file [src/web/personnes.controller.ts]:

import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, ParseIntPipe, Post, Redirect, Render, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { MetierException } from '../metier/metier.exception';
import { PersonnesMetier } from '../metier/personnes.metier';
import { flash } from './flash';
import { FormulairePersonneDto } from './formulaire-personne.dto';
import { validerFormulaire } from './validation';

// the WEB layer: read the request, call the business layer, select the view
@Controller()
export class PersonnesController {
  constructor(private readonly metier: PersonnesMetier) {}

  @Get()
  @Redirect('/personnes')
  racine(): void {}

  @Get('personnes')
  @Render('liste')
  async liste(): Promise<object> {
    return { personnes: await this.metier.lister() };
  }

  @Get('personnes/ajouter')
  @Render('formulaire')
  formulaireAjout(): object {
    return { titre: 'Ajouter une personne', action: '/personnes/ajouter', valeurs: {}, erreurs: {} };
  }

  @Post('personnes/ajouter')
  async ajouter(@Body() corps: Record<string, string>, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    const vue = { titre: 'Ajouter une personne', action: '/personnes/ajouter' };
    const { dto, erreurs } = await validerFormulaire(FormulairePersonneDto, corps);
    if (Object.keys(erreurs).length > 0) {
      res.render('formulaire', { ...vue, valeurs: corps, erreurs, erreur: 'Le formulaire contient des erreurs.' });
      return;
    }
    try {
      const p = await this.metier.ajouter(dto);
      flash(res, { type: 'success', texte: `${p.prenom} ${p.nom} a été ajouté(e).` });
      res.redirect('/personnes');
    } catch (e) {
       // A business rule rejected the addition: the form is redisplayed
      if (!(e instanceof MetierException)) throw e;
      res.render('formulaire', { ...vue, valeurs: corps, erreurs: {}, erreur: e.message });
    }
  }

  @Get('personnes/:id/modifier')
  @Render('formulaire')
  async formulaireModification(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number): Promise<object> {
    const p = await this.metier.lire(id);
    return { titre: 'Modifier une personne', action: `/personnes/${id}/modifier`, valeurs: p, erreurs: {} };
  }

  @Post('personnes/:id/modifier')
  async modifier(
    @Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number,
    @Body() corps: Record<string, string>,
    @Res() res: Response,
  ): Promise<void> {
    const vue = { titre: 'Modifier une personne', action: `/personnes/${id}/modifier` };
    const { dto, erreurs } = await validerFormulaire(FormulairePersonneDto, corps);
    if (Object.keys(erreurs).length > 0) {
      res.render('formulaire', { ...vue, valeurs: corps, erreurs, erreur: 'Le formulaire contient des erreurs.' });
      return;
    }
    try {
      const p = await this.metier.modifier(id, Number(corps.version), dto);
      flash(res, { type: 'success', texte: `${p.prenom} ${p.nom} a été modifié(e).` });
      res.redirect('/personnes');
    } catch (e) {
      if (!(e instanceof MetierException)) throw e;
      res.render('formulaire', { ...vue, valeurs: corps, erreurs: {}, erreur: e.message });
    }
  }

  @Post('personnes/:id/supprimer')
  async supprimer(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    try {
      const p = await this.metier.supprimer(id);
      flash(res, { type: 'success', texte: `${p.prenom} ${p.nom} a été supprimé(e).` });
    } catch (e) {
      if (!(e instanceof MetierException)) throw e;
       // No form to redisplay: the error is also displayed instantly
      flash(res, { type: 'danger', texte: e.message });
    }
    res.redirect('/personnes');
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 12: the controller only knows the business layer;
  • lines 14–16: the site root redirects to the list;
  • lines 18–22: an asynchronous action: the list is retrieved from the database;
  • lines 30–47: the addition, in three steps: form validation (errors → page reload), call to the business layer (success → pop-up message and redirection), [MetierException] (→ page reload with the message at the bottom of the page). Another exception is thrown ([throw e]): this is an anomaly, which the exception filter for [NestJS] will convert into a 500 error;
  • lines 49–54: the update form, pre-filled with the record retrieved from the database (including its version);
  • lines 56–61: same process as for adding a record; the version returned by the form is passed to the business layer;
  • lines 78–89: deletion. There is no form to redisplay: any errors are also included in the flash message.

The file [src/app.module.ts]:

import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { configBase } from './config/database.config';
import { PersonnesDao } from './dao/personnes.dao';
import { Personne } from './entities/personne.entity';
import { PersonnesMetier } from './metier/personnes.metier';
import { PersonnesController } from './web/personnes.controller';

@Module({
  imports: [
     // the database connection, for the entire application
    TypeOrmModule.forRoot(configBase()),
     // the injectable Repository<T>s in this module
    TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Personne]),
  ],
  controllers: [PersonnesController],
   // the three layers: web (controller) -> business logic -> DAO
  providers: [PersonnesMetier, PersonnesDao],
})
export class AppModule {}
  • line 12: the database connection for the entire application;
  • line 14: enables the [Repository<Personne>] to be injected;
  • line 18: the business layer services and DAO.

The [views/formulaire.hbs] file:

<h1 class="h3">{{titre}}</h1>
<form method="post" action="{{action}}" novalidate>
  {{!-- la version de la fiche lue, renvoyée avec la modification --}}
  <input type="hidden" name="version" value="{{valeurs.version}}">
  <div class="row g-2 mb-3">
    <div class="col-sm-5">
      <label class="form-label" for="prenom">Prénom</label>
